questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: How one generation of selection against a recessive phenotype shifts allele frequency away from Hardy–Weinberg values
questions.question: In a large, randomly mating population, 16 % of individuals show a recessive phenotype (aa). For one generation, all aa individuals are prevented from breeding, while AA and Aa breed at random. What is the frequency of allele a among the breeding parents, and about what percentage of the next generation will be aa?
options: A) 0.40; 16 %, since Hardy–Weinberg proportions are always kept
B) About 0.29; about 8 %, because selection against aa changes the allele frequency, violating a Hardy–Weinberg condition
C) 0; 0 %, because all recessive alleles are removed in one generation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) q ≈ 0.29; about 8 % aa in the next generation.
Concept: The Hardy–Weinberg principle states that allele and genotype frequencies stay constant from generation to generation (p² + 2pq + q² = 1) if there is no mutation, no migration (gene flow), no genetic drift, random mating and no natural selection. Any of these factors disturbs the equilibrium and causes evolution.
Given: q² = 0.16, so q = 0.40 and p = 0.60; AA = 0.36, Aa = 0.48, aa = 0.16.
Formula/Principle: among breeders, q′ = (frequency of a alleles) ÷ (all alleles) = (½ × Aa) ÷ (AA + Aa).
Step 1: Breeders: AA 0.36 + Aa 0.48 = 0.84; a alleles = ½ × 0.48 = 0.24; q′ = 0.24 ÷ 0.84 ≈ 0.286 (equivalently q′ = q/(1 + q) = 0.4/1.4).
Step 2: Next generation (random mating): aa = q′² ≈ 0.082, about 8 %.
Why: The a allele survives in heterozygotes, which are not removed, so the recessive phenotype falls but does not disappear; selection against a rare recessive becomes slower each generation because most a alleles hide in carriers.
Why not the others: (A) Selection is acting, so the frequencies do change. (C) The 48 % heterozygotes still carry a. (D) Halves q instead of calculating it from the breeders.
Key point: Selection against aa: q′ = q/(1 + q); carriers keep the allele in the population.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the source and action of opioids, cannabinoids and cocaine
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares commonly abused drugs?
options: A) Heroin (smack), obtained by acetylation of morphine from the poppy Papaver somniferum, is a depressant that binds opioid receptors in the central nervous system and gut; cocaine, from the coca plant, interferes with the transport of dopamine and stimulates the central nervous system; cannabinoids from Cannabis sativa mainly affect the cardiovascular system
B) Heroin is a stimulant obtained from the coca plant
C) Cocaine slows down body functions by binding opioid receptors
D) Cannabinoids are synthetic drugs that have no natural source
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Heroin: depressant from morphine, acts on opioid receptors; cocaine: dopamine-transport blocker and stimulant; cannabinoids: cardiovascular effects.
Concept: Drugs are grouped by source and action. Opioids (morphine, heroin) bind specific opioid receptors and depress body functions. Cannabinoids (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja) come from the inflorescences of Cannabis sativa and act on cannabinoid receptors, mainly in the brain. Cocaine (coke, crack) comes from Erythroxylum coca and has a strong stimulating action, giving euphoria and, in excess, hallucinations.
Why: Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is made chemically from morphine; it slows breathing and heart rate. Cocaine blocks the re-uptake of dopamine, so dopamine stays longer at synapses. Repeated use of these drugs causes tolerance and dependence.
Why not the others: (B) Heroin comes from the poppy and is a depressant. (C) Cocaine is a stimulant and acts on dopamine transport, not opioid receptors. (D) Cannabinoids occur naturally in Cannabis.
Key point: Opioids depress (poppy); cocaine stimulates (coca, dopamine); cannabinoids from Cannabis affect the heart and blood vessels.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Identifying recombinant colonies by insertional inactivation of the tetracycline-resistance gene in pBR322
questions.question: Foreign DNA is inserted into the BamHI site of the plasmid pBR322, which lies within the tetracycline-resistance gene (tet^R); the ampicillin-resistance gene (amp^R) is left intact. E. coli cells are transformed and spread on an ampicillin plate, and the colonies are then replica-plated onto a tetracycline plate. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Colonies that grow on tetracycline are the recombinants
B) Only untransformed cells grow on ampicillin
C) Recombinant plasmids lack an origin of replication, so they cannot multiply

D) All colonies on ampicillin carry a plasmid; those that fail to grow on tetracycline carry recombinant plasmids, because the insert has inactivated tet^R (insertional inactivation); colonies that grow on both carry the plasmid without an insert
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Colonies growing on ampicillin but not on tetracycline are recombinants.
Concept: A cloning vector needs an origin of replication (ori), which controls copy number; selectable markers, such as antibiotic-resistance genes, to pick out transformants; and unique cloning sites. Inserting DNA into a marker gene destroys its function (insertional inactivation), which distinguishes recombinants from non-recombinants.
Why: Untransformed E. coli is sensitive to both antibiotics, so only cells with a plasmid grow on ampicillin. A plasmid with an insert in tet^R no longer gives tetracycline resistance, so those colonies are missing on the replica plate. Plasmids that re-closed without an insert keep both resistances.
Why not the others: (A) Growth on tetracycline means tet^R is intact, so there is no insert. (B) Untransformed cells lack amp^R and die on ampicillin. (C) The insert is in tet^R; ori is not affected.
Key point: Insert in tet^R gives amp^R tet^S recombinants; select on ampicillin, screen on tetracycline.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Measuring asymmetric competition from the fall in population density of two species grown together
questions.question: Two species X and Y feed on the same resource. Grown separately, X reaches a stable density of 400 per plot and Y of 250 per plot. Grown together, X stabilises at 300 and Y at 50. What is the percentage reduction in density for each species, and what do the results show?
options: A) X 75 %, Y 20 %; X is harmed more
B) X 25 %, Y 80 %; this is predation, with X preying on Y
C) X 25 %, Y 80 %; both are harmed (−/−), so it is competition, which is asymmetric because Y is affected much more, and with time Y may be excluded (Gause's competitive exclusion principle)
D) X 0 %, Y 100 %; only Y is affected, so it is amensalism
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) X falls by 25 %, Y by 80 %; asymmetric competition.
Concept: In interspecific competition both species are harmed (−/−), because each reduces the resources available to the other. Competition is often asymmetric: one species suffers far more. Gause's principle states that two species competing for the same limiting resource cannot coexist indefinitely; the inferior competitor is eventually eliminated, unless the species partition the resource.
Given: X: 400 alone, 300 together; Y: 250 alone, 50 together.
Formula/Principle: percentage reduction = (alone − together) ÷ alone × 100.
Step 1: X: (400 − 300) ÷ 400 × 100 = 25 %.
Step 2: Y: (250 − 50) ÷ 250 × 100 = 80 %.
Why: Both densities fall in mixed culture, so each harms the other; the much larger fall in Y shows that X is the superior competitor.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the two percentages. (B) Predation is +/−; nothing shows X gaining, since its density falls too. (D) X is reduced by 25 %, so it is also affected.
Key point: Competition is −/−, often asymmetric; strong competition can exclude the weaker species.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Using Whittaker's criteria to explain why fungi form a kingdom separate from plants
questions.question: Which statement correctly uses Whittaker's criteria to separate Kingdom Fungi from Kingdom Plantae?
options: A) Both are eukaryotic and have cell walls, but fungi have walls of chitin and are heterotrophic (absorbing food as saprophytes or parasites), while plants have cellulose walls and are autotrophic; Whittaker used cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships to define kingdoms
B) Fungi are prokaryotic and plants are eukaryotic
C) Fungi and plants are placed in separate kingdoms only because fungi are always unicellular
D) Fungi photosynthesise using chlorophyll stored in hyphae
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Fungi: chitin wall, heterotrophic by absorption; plants: cellulose wall, autotrophic.
Concept: R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. His criteria were cell structure (prokaryotic or eukaryotic), body organisation (unicellular or multicellular), mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships. Earlier, the two-kingdom system had placed fungi with plants because both have cell walls.
Why: Fungi lack chlorophyll and take in dissolved organic food from dead matter or a host. Their walls contain chitin and polysaccharides. Plants are mostly autotrophic with chlorophyll and cellulose walls. These differences in nutrition and wall composition justify a separate kingdom.
Why not the others: (B) Both fungi and plants are eukaryotic. (C) Most fungi are multicellular (yeast is an exception). (D) Fungi lack chlorophyll and are heterotrophic.
Key point: Five-kingdom criteria: cell type, body organisation, nutrition, reproduction, phylogeny; fungi are heterotrophic with chitin walls.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting heart chambers, operculum and internal fertilisation across a cartilaginous fish, a bony fish and a frog
questions.question: Consider Scoliodon (dogfish), Labeo (rohu) and Rana (frog). What is the total number of heart chambers in the three animals together, how many of them have gills covered by an operculum, and how many show internal fertilisation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 7 chambers; 1 with an operculum; 1 with internal fertilisation.
Concept: Fishes have a two-chambered heart (one auricle, one ventricle). Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes, such as Scoliodon) have 5–7 pairs of separate gill slits without an operculum, placoid scales and internal fertilisation (males have claspers). Bony fishes (Osteichthyes, such as Labeo) have four pairs of gills covered by an operculum, an air bladder and usually external fertilisation. Amphibians (such as Rana) have a three-chambered heart (two auricles, one ventricle) and external fertilisation.
Given: Scoliodon, Labeo, Rana.
Formula/Principle: add the chambers; count each feature.
Step 1: Heart chambers: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7.
Step 2: Operculum: Labeo only = 1. Internal fertilisation: Scoliodon only = 1.
Why: The operculum covers the gills only in bony fishes; claspers allow internal fertilisation in cartilaginous fishes; the frog releases eggs and sperm into water.
Why not the others: (A) Gives the frog a four-chambered heart and an operculum to the dogfish. (B) Gives the frog only two chambers and counts the frog as fertilised internally. (D) Gives all three animals internal fertilisation and two an operculum.
Key point: Fishes: 2-chambered heart; operculum only in bony fishes; cartilaginous fishes fertilise internally; frogs: 3-chambered heart, external fertilisation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the mixing of membrane proteins after fusing human and mouse cells as evidence for the fluid mosaic model
questions.question: A human cell, whose membrane proteins are labelled with a green fluorescent dye, is fused with a mouse cell, whose membrane proteins are labelled red. At 37 °C the two colours are completely intermixed over the surface of the hybrid cell within about 40 minutes, even when protein synthesis is blocked; at 15 °C the colours stay in separate halves. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) New proteins are made in the hybrid cell and inserted evenly into the membrane
B) Membrane proteins are fixed in position by the cell wall
C) The membrane consists of a single layer of protein with no lipid
D) Membrane proteins can move sideways within a fluid lipid bilayer (fluid mosaic model); this lateral movement depends on membrane fluidity, which falls at low temperature
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Proteins diffuse laterally in a fluid bilayer; fluidity falls at low temperature.
Concept: In the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972), the membrane is a quasi-fluid lipid bilayer in which proteins are embedded (integral) or attached (peripheral). The lipids and many proteins can move sideways within the plane of the membrane. This fluidity is important for cell growth, the formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.
Why: Mixing without protein synthesis shows that existing proteins moved, not that new ones were made. The temperature dependence shows that movement depends on the fluid state of the lipids, which becomes more rigid when cooled.
Why not the others: (A) Mixing still happened when protein synthesis was blocked. (B) Animal cells have no cell wall, and the result shows the proteins are not fixed. (C) The membrane is a lipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it.
Key point: Fluid mosaic model: lipid bilayer with laterally mobile proteins; fluidity depends on temperature.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the hydrogen bonding and melting temperature of two double-stranded DNA samples with different base compositions
questions.question: Two double-stranded DNA samples each contain 1000 base pairs. In sample X adenine makes up 30 % of the bases; in sample Y adenine makes up 20 %. How many hydrogen bonds hold each sample's strands together, and which sample is more likely to come from a bacterium living in hot springs?
options: B) X 2400, Y 2600; Y, because its higher G≡C content needs more energy (a higher temperature) to separate the strands
C) Both 2500; neither
D) X 2400, Y 2600; X, because A=T pairs are more stable
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) X has 2400 and Y has 2600 hydrogen bonds; Y is from the hot-spring bacterium.
Concept: In double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds and G pairs with C by three (Chargaff's rules: A = T, G = C). DNA with more G≡C pairs has more hydrogen bonds (and stronger base stacking), so it needs a higher temperature to separate its strands.
Given: X: A = 30 %, so T = 30 % and G = C = 20 %; Y: A = 20 %, so T = 20 % and G = C = 30 %. Each sample has 1000 bp.
Formula/Principle: H-bonds = 2 × (A–T pairs) + 3 × (G–C pairs).
Step 1: X: 600 A–T pairs and 400 G–C pairs: 2(600) + 3(400) = 2400.
Step 2: Y: 400 A–T pairs and 600 G–C pairs: 2(400) + 3(600) = 2600.
Why: Organisms living at high temperatures tend to have DNA rich in G≡C pairs, which remains double-stranded at temperatures that would separate A=T-rich DNA.
Why not the others: (A) Swaps the counts: more A means fewer hydrogen bonds. (C) Ignores the different base compositions. (D) The counts are right, but A=T pairs, with two hydrogen bonds, are less stable than G≡C pairs.
Key point: A=T has 2 hydrogen bonds, G≡C has 3; more GC means more stable DNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Assigning eight enzymes to the six enzyme classes and counting the hydrolases
questions.question: The following enzymes are classified into the six classes of enzymes: amylase, DNA ligase, aldolase, hexokinase, pepsin, alcohol dehydrogenase, lipase and phosphohexose isomerase. How many of them are hydrolases, and how many of the six classes are represented in the list?
options: A) 4 hydrolases; 5 classes
B) 2 hydrolases; 4 classes
C) 3 hydrolases; 5 classes
D) 3 hydrolases; all 6 classes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3 hydrolases; all 6 classes are represented.
Concept: Enzymes are grouped into six classes: oxidoreductases (dehydrogenases; transfer of electrons or hydrogen), transferases (transfer a group other than hydrogen), hydrolases (break bonds by adding water), lyases (remove groups without hydrolysis, often leaving double bonds), isomerases (interconvert isomers) and ligases (join two molecules, using ATP).
Given: eight enzymes.
Formula/Principle: assign each enzyme by the reaction it catalyses.
Step 1: Hydrolases: amylase (starch), pepsin (proteins), lipase (fats) = 3.
Step 2: Ligase: DNA ligase; lyase: aldolase (splits fructose bisphosphate); transferase: hexokinase (transfers phosphate from ATP); oxidoreductase: alcohol dehydrogenase; isomerase: phosphohexose isomerase. All six classes appear.
Why: Digestive enzymes are typical hydrolases. Hexokinase moves a phosphate group, so it is a transferase, not a ligase.
Why not the others: (A) Counts hexokinase or aldolase as a hydrolase. (B) Misses one of the digestive hydrolases and several classes. (C) Misses one class; each of the six is represented once outside the hydrolases.
Key point: Six classes: oxidoreductase, transferase, hydrolase, lyase, isomerase, ligase.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Minimum photons and oxygen released to supply the NADPH for fixing six molecules of carbon dioxide by non-cyclic electron flow
questions.question: Making one molecule of glucose (fixing 6 CO₂) in the Calvin cycle uses 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. If all the NADPH comes from non-cyclic electron flow, in which each electron passing from water to NADP⁺ must absorb one photon at PSII and one at PSI, what is the minimum number of photons absorbed, and how many molecules of O₂ are released?
options: A) 48 photons; 6 O₂
B) 24 photons; 12 O₂
C) 12 photons; 6 O₂
D) 48 photons; 12 O₂
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 48 photons; 6 O₂.
Concept: In non-cyclic photophosphorylation (the Z scheme), water is split at PSII (2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻), and electrons pass through the cytochrome b₆f complex to PSI and then to NADP⁺. Each NADPH needs two electrons. A proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane drives ATP synthesis by ATP synthase (chemiosmosis). Cyclic flow around PSI makes extra ATP only.
Given: 12 NADPH needed; 2 photons per electron (one at each photosystem).
Formula/Principle: electrons = 2 × NADPH; photons = 2 × electrons; O₂ = electrons ÷ 4.
Step 1: Electrons = 2 × 12 = 24; photons = 2 × 24 = 48.
Step 2: O₂ = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 (from 12 H₂O).
Why: The 6 O₂ released match the 6 CO₂ fixed in the overall equation of photosynthesis. Non-cyclic flow alone may not give enough ATP for the 18 required, so cyclic flow supplies the rest.
Why not the others: (B) Counts one photon per electron, and 12 O₂ would need 48 electrons. (C) Counts one photon per NADPH. (D) The photon count is right, but each O₂ releases four electrons, so only 6 O₂ are produced.
Key point: 1 NADPH = 2 e⁻ = 4 photons (non-cyclic); 4 e⁻ per O₂.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Contrasting how abscisic acid and ethylene act during water stress, dormancy, senescence and growth
questions.question: Which statement about abscisic acid (ABA) and ethylene is correct?
options: A) ABA promotes seed germination and acts like gibberellin
B) Ethylene is a gas that inhibits fruit ripening and delays senescence

C) ABA, produced in larger amounts in water stress, makes stomata close and induces seed and bud dormancy, generally opposing gibberellins; ethylene, a gaseous hormone, promotes senescence, abscission of leaves and flowers and fruit ripening, and causes horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation
D) ABA and ethylene both cause rapid cell elongation of internodes in all plants
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ABA: stress hormone (stomatal closure, dormancy); ethylene: senescence, abscission, ripening, triple response.
Concept: ABA is a growth inhibitor, called the stress hormone because it increases plant tolerance to stresses. It causes stomatal closure by making guard cells lose K⁺ and water, and it maintains seed dormancy, letting seeds survive dry periods. Ethylene, a simple gaseous hormone, is produced by ripening fruits and senescing tissues; ethephon is used to release ethylene in agriculture.
Why: In drought, a rise in ABA closes stomata quickly, saving water. ABA and gibberellin act antagonistically in seed germination. Ethylene increases the rate of respiration during fruit ripening (respiratory climacteric) and promotes the formation of the abscission layer.
Why not the others: (A) ABA inhibits germination and acts against gibberellin. (B) Ethylene promotes, not inhibits, ripening and senescence. (D) ABA inhibits growth; ethylene usually reduces stem elongation.
Key point: ABA closes stomata and causes dormancy; ethylene ripens fruit and promotes senescence and abscission.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the ventilation response to breathing extra carbon dioxide compared with breathing less oxygen
questions.question:
A resting subject breathes three gas mixtures for ten minutes each, and the volume of air breathed per minute is measured.
| Mixture | Ventilation (L min⁻¹) |
|---|---|
| Normal air | 6 |
| Air with 5 % CO₂ (normal O₂) | 25 |
| Air with 15 % O₂ (normal CO₂) | 7 |
Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) A fall in O₂ is the main stimulus to breathing

B) A rise in CO₂ is a strong stimulus: CO₂ and H⁺ excite the chemosensitive area next to the respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla, which increases breathing; receptors in the aortic arch and carotid arteries also respond, but a moderate fall in O₂ has only a small effect
C) Breathing is controlled only by the pneumotaxic centre in the pons, which is insensitive to blood gases
D) The results show that the subject has emphysema
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) CO₂ (through H⁺) acting on the medullary chemosensitive area is the main stimulus.
Concept: The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla sets the basic breathing rhythm; the pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate it. A chemosensitive area next to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺; when they rise, it signals the rhythm centre to increase ventilation so that they are removed. Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid arteries also detect CO₂ and H⁺. The role of O₂ in regulating breathing is quite insignificant under normal conditions.
Why: 5 % CO₂ increased ventilation fourfold, whereas reducing O₂ to 15 % made little difference.
Why not the others: (A) The O₂ change caused only a small increase. (C) The pneumotaxic centre moderates the rhythm; blood gases act through chemoreceptors. (D) Emphysema (damaged alveolar walls, often from smoking) is not shown by this normal response.
Key point: Breathing is driven mainly by CO₂ and H⁺ acting on the medullary chemosensitive area.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Matching ECG waves to events of the cardiac cycle and interpreting a prolonged P–R interval
questions.question: The table summarises parts of the ECG of a patient. P–Q (P–R) interval: 0.32 s (normal 0.12–0.20 s); QRS complex: normal; T wave: normal. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The P wave shows depolarisation of the atria started by the SA node, the QRS complex shows depolarisation of the ventricles (marking the start of ventricular systole), and the T wave shows ventricular repolarisation (end of systole); the long P–R interval suggests that the impulse is delayed in passing from the atria to the ventricles through the AV node
B) The P wave shows ventricular repolarisation, and the long P–R interval shows that the ventricles contract too early
C) The QRS complex shows the closing of the semilunar valves
D) The T wave shows contraction of the atria
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P: atrial depolarisation; QRS: ventricular depolarisation; T: ventricular repolarisation; long P–R: delayed AV conduction.
Concept: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart. The P wave represents excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, which leads to atrial contraction. The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation, which starts ventricular contraction. The T wave represents the return of the ventricles to the resting state. The P–R interval is the time for the impulse to travel from the SA node through the atria, the AV node and the bundle of His.
Why: The normal P–R interval is about 0.12–0.20 s; 0.32 s means abnormally slow conduction through the AV node. Any deviation in the shape or timing of the ECG indicates a possible abnormality, which is why the ECG is clinically important. The heart's rhythm is normally set by the SA node and adjusted by the autonomic nervous system.
Why not the others: (B) The P wave is atrial depolarisation, and a long P–R interval means delay, not early contraction. (C) The QRS complex is electrical, not a valve sound. (D) The T wave is ventricular repolarisation; atrial repolarisation is hidden in the QRS complex.
Key point: P = atrial depolarisation, QRS = ventricular depolarisation, T = ventricular repolarisation; P–R = AV conduction time.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Effect of damage to the hypothalamus–posterior pituitary on ADH and urine, and the reflex that empties the bladder
questions.question: After a head injury, a patient passes very large volumes of dilute urine and feels constantly thirsty, although blood glucose is normal. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) The patient has excess ADH, which blocks water reabsorption in the kidney
B) The glomerular filtration rate has fallen to zero
C) Insulin deficiency has caused glucose to appear in the urine

D) Damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary has reduced release of ADH (vasopressin), so the distal tubule and collecting duct reabsorb less water (diabetes insipidus); bladder emptying itself is a reflex, in which stretch receptors in the bladder wall signal the CNS, causing the detrusor muscle to contract and the urethral sphincter to relax
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Reduced ADH causes diabetes insipidus; micturition is a stretch reflex.
Concept: ADH (vasopressin) is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. When body fluid volume falls or osmolarity rises, osmoreceptors trigger ADH release; ADH makes the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct more permeable to water, so concentrated urine is produced. Without ADH, water reabsorption in these parts falls, giving large volumes of dilute urine (diuresis). Alcohol also inhibits ADH release, which is why it increases urine flow.
Why: Normal blood glucose rules out diabetes mellitus. The urine is dilute because the collecting ducts cannot reabsorb water without ADH. When urine collects, the bladder wall stretches; signals to the CNS bring about contraction of the smooth muscle of the bladder and relaxation of the sphincter (the micturition reflex).
Why not the others: (A) Excess ADH would increase water reabsorption, giving small volumes of concentrated urine. (B) With no filtration there would be no urine at all. (C) Blood glucose is normal, so this is not diabetes mellitus.
Key point: ADH increases water reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct; lack of ADH gives diabetes insipidus.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Erythropoietin from the kidney at high altitude, and the hormones made by the heart and the gut
questions.question: A climber spends several weeks at high altitude, and the red blood cell count rises. Which explanation, together with a correct statement about hormones of non-endocrine organs, is right?
options: A) The rise is caused by gastrin released from the heart in response to low oxygen

B) Low oxygen stimulates cells of the kidney (juxtaglomerular cells) to secrete erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell formation in the bone marrow; the atrial wall of the heart secretes atrial natriuretic factor, which lowers blood pressure; the gut secretes gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin and gastric inhibitory peptide
C) Secretin from the stomach stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells
D) The testis secretes erythropoietin when oxygen is low
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Kidney erythropoietin stimulates erythropoiesis; heart makes ANF; gut makes gastrin, secretin, CCK and GIP.
Concept: Besides the endocrine glands, some organs have tissues that secrete hormones. The juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce erythropoietin, which stimulates erythropoiesis (formation of RBCs). The atrial wall of the heart secretes atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), which dilates blood vessels and so reduces blood pressure. Gastrointestinal hormones include gastrin (stimulates gastric glands to secrete HCl and pepsinogen), secretin (stimulates the pancreas to secrete water and bicarbonate), cholecystokinin (stimulates secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile) and GIP (inhibits gastric secretion and motility). The gonads secrete sex hormones (androgens from the Leydig cells of the testis; oestrogen and progesterone from the ovary).
Why: At high altitude, the lower partial pressure of oxygen reduces oxygen delivery to the kidney; the resulting rise in erythropoietin increases the RBC count, improving oxygen transport.
Why not the others: (A) Gastrin is a gut hormone that acts on gastric glands, not on the bone marrow. (C) Secretin acts on the pancreas. (D) The testis secretes androgens, not erythropoietin.
Key point: Erythropoietin (kidney) → RBCs; ANF (heart) lowers BP; gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP (gut).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting pollination experiments with compatible and incompatible pollen, and the ploidy of the products of double fertilisation
questions.question: In a plant with 2n = 24, three emasculated and bagged flowers are dusted with different pollen. Flower 1, with pollen from another plant of the same species: pollen tubes grow down the style and seeds form. Flower 2, with pollen from an unrelated species: the pollen fails to germinate. Flower 3, with its own pollen (the plant is self-incompatible): the pollen tubes stop growing in the style. Which interpretation, with the correct chromosome numbers, is right?
options: A) Pollen always germinates on any stigma; the failures are due to lack of water
B) The pistil accepts every pollen grain, and the endosperm has 24 chromosomes

C) The pistil recognises compatible pollen through chemical interactions between pollen and pistil and blocks incompatible pollen at the stigma or style; after compatible pollination, double fertilisation gives a zygote with 24 chromosomes and a primary endosperm nucleus with 36 chromosomes
D) Self-pollen is always successful, and the zygote formed has 36 chromosomes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Pollen–pistil recognition blocks incompatible pollen; zygote 2n = 24, endosperm 3n = 36.
Concept: The pistil can recognise its own species' compatible pollen and reject others through chemical interactions between components of the pollen and the pistil (pollen–pistil interaction). Rejection stops germination on the stigma or pollen-tube growth in the style. In double fertilisation, one male gamete fuses with the egg (syngamy, giving the diploid zygote) and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (triple fusion, giving the triploid primary endosperm nucleus).
Why: Flower 1 shows normal compatibility. Flower 2 shows interspecific rejection at the stigma. Flower 3 shows self-incompatibility, a device that prevents inbreeding. With n = 12: zygote 12 + 12 = 24; endosperm 12 + 12 + 12 = 36. Emasculation and bagging ensured that only the chosen pollen reached each stigma.
Why not the others: (A) All flowers were treated alike; rejection is chemical, not a lack of water. (B) Flowers 2 and 3 show rejection, and endosperm is triploid. (D) Self-pollen was rejected in flower 3, and the zygote is diploid (24).
Key point: Pistil recognises compatible pollen; zygote 2n, endosperm 3n.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading cell number and cell size during early cleavage of a human embryo, and identifying the morula
questions.question:
The table gives the number of cells and the average cell diameter of an early human embryo at different times after fertilisation.
| Time after fertilisation | Number of cells | Average cell diameter (µm) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 h | 1 | 100 |
| about 30 h | 2 | 79 |
| about 40 h | 4 | 63 |
| about 60 h | 8 | 50 |
| about 72 h | 16 | 40 |
Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) The cells grow to full size between divisions

B) The divisions are mitotic and occur without growth, so the total volume stays about the same while the volume of each cell halves at each division; the embryo with 8–16 cells is the morula, which moves into the uterus and becomes a blastocyst that implants in the endometrium
C) Each cell division is meiotic, halving the chromosome number
D) The 16-cell embryo is the blastocyst, which has already implanted
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cleavage without growth; cell volume halves per division; 8–16 cells is the morula.
Concept: The zygote divides by mitosis (cleavage) as it moves through the isthmus of the oviduct towards the uterus, forming 2, 4, 8 and 16 daughter cells called blastomeres. The embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is called a morula. It continues to divide and becomes a blastocyst, with an outer trophoblast and an inner cell mass; the trophoblast attaches to the endometrium (implantation), and the inner cell mass becomes the embryo.
Why: If the total volume is constant, each cell's volume halves at each division, and its diameter falls by a factor of 2^(1/3) ≈ 1.26: 100 → 79 → 63 → 50 → 40 µm, exactly as in the table. So the cells do not grow between divisions.
Why not the others: (A) Cell diameter falls steadily, so there is no growth. (C) Cleavage is mitotic; the cells stay diploid. (D) A 16-cell embryo is a morula; implantation occurs later, at the blastocyst stage.
Key point: Cleavage: mitosis without growth; 8–16 cells = morula; blastocyst implants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Using co-dominance and multiple alleles of the ABO gene to settle a parentage question
questions.question: A woman of blood group A has a child of blood group O. A man of blood group AB is named as the father. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) The man could be the father, because AB includes every allele
B) The child must have blood group AB if the man is the father
C) Blood group O shows that the mother must be homozygous I^A I^A
D) The man cannot be the father: the child is ii, so it must have received i from each parent, but a man of group AB (I^A I^B) can pass on only I^A or I^B; the mother must be I^A i
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The man cannot be the father; the mother is I^A i.
Concept: The ABO gene has three alleles (multiple alleles): I^A and I^B are co-dominant (both are expressed in I^A I^B, giving group AB), and both are dominant over i. Group O is ii; group A is I^A I^A or I^A i; group B is I^B I^B or I^B i.
Why: An O child (ii) needs one i from each parent. The mother, being group A, must be I^A i. A man of group AB has no i allele, so every child of his would be group A, B or AB. Blood tests can therefore exclude parentage, though they cannot prove it.
Why not the others: (A) Having both I^A and I^B means having no i, so he cannot give an O child. (B) Children of an I^A i mother and an I^A I^B father could be A, AB or B, not only AB. (C) An I^A I^A mother could not give i.
Key point: I^A and I^B co-dominant, i recessive; an O child needs i from both parents.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Writing the mRNA and template strand from a coding strand, and the effect of a point mutation that creates a stop codon
questions.question: A short coding strand of DNA reads 5′-ATG GCT TGG-3′. Which statement about its transcript and a mutation in it is correct?
options: A) The mRNA is 5′-AUG GCU UGG-3′, the template strand is 3′-TAC CGA ACC-5′, and a mutation changing the last G of TGG to A on the coding strand gives the mRNA codon UGA, a stop codon, so a shortened protein is made
B) The mRNA is 5′-UAC CGA ACC-3′, copied from the coding strand
C) The mRNA contains thymine in place of uracil
D) Changing TGG to TGA has no effect, because the genetic code is degenerate
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) mRNA 5′-AUG GCU UGG-3′; template 3′-TAC CGA ACC-5′; TGG → TGA creates the stop codon UGA.
Concept: The two DNA strands are complementary (A–T, G–C) and antiparallel. RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3′ → 5′ and makes mRNA 5′ → 3′, so the mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U in place of T. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.
Why: Coding 5′-ATG GCT TGG-3′ gives mRNA 5′-AUG GCU UGG-3′ (Met–Ala–Trp). A single-base substitution that changes UGG (Trp) to UGA ends translation early (a nonsense mutation).
Why not the others: (B) The mRNA matches the coding strand, not its complement. (C) RNA contains uracil, not thymine. (D) UGA is a stop codon, not another codon for tryptophan; degeneracy does not apply here.
Key point: mRNA = coding strand with U for T; a substitution creating a stop codon shortens the protein.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Length of DNA in a human diploid cell and in E. coli, and the number of nucleosomes needed to package human DNA
questions.question: A human diploid cell contains about 6.6 × 10⁹ base pairs of DNA, and E. coli has about 4.6 × 10⁶ base pairs. The distance between adjacent base pairs is 0.34 nm, and one nucleosome (with linker) contains about 200 base pairs. What is the total length of DNA in a human diploid cell, the length of the E. coli DNA, and the approximate number of nucleosomes in a human diploid cell?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.2 m; 1.36 mm; 3.3 × 10⁷ nucleosomes.
Concept: DNA in eukaryotes is wrapped around a core of eight histone molecules (an octamer of positively charged histones) to form nucleosomes, each containing about 200 bp including linker DNA. Nucleosomes form a "beads on a string" structure that coils further into chromatin fibres. In prokaryotes, the negatively charged DNA is held by positively charged proteins in the nucleoid.
Given: 6.6 × 10⁹ bp (human); 4.6 × 10⁶ bp (E. coli); 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m per bp; 200 bp per nucleosome.
Formula/Principle: length = number of bp × 0.34 nm; nucleosomes = bp ÷ 200.
Step 1: Human: 6.6 × 10⁹ × 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m ≈ 2.2 m.
Step 2: E. coli: 4.6 × 10⁶ × 0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m ≈ 1.36 × 10⁻³ m = 1.36 mm.
Step 3: Nucleosomes: 6.6 × 10⁹ ÷ 200 = 3.3 × 10⁷.
Why: About 2 m of DNA must fit into a nucleus about 10⁻⁵ m across, so packaging by histones is essential.
Why not the others: (A) Uses 0.34 pm instead of 0.34 nm, and divides by 2 instead of 200. (B) Multiplies the length by 10 and uses wrong units. (D) Counts one nucleosome per base pair.
Key point: Length = bp × 0.34 nm; one nucleosome ≈ 200 bp.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Why chromium and copper have anomalous configurations, and why nitrogen has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than oxygen
questions.question: Which statement correctly explains the extra stability of half-filled and completely filled subshells?
options: A) Chromium is [Ar]3d⁴4s² and copper is [Ar]3d⁹4s², because the 4s orbital must always be filled first
B) Oxygen has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than nitrogen, because it has a larger nuclear charge

C) Chromium is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and copper is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹, because half-filled and completely filled d subshells are extra stable, owing to their symmetrical distribution of electrons and maximum exchange energy; for the same reason, nitrogen (2p³, half-filled) has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than oxygen (2p⁴), whose electron is removed from a doubly occupied orbital
D) Half-filled subshells are less stable, because unpaired electrons repel one another strongly
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Cr 3d⁵4s¹ and Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹; exchange energy and symmetry; N has a higher IE₁ than O.
Concept: Exchange energy is the stabilisation that results when electrons of the same spin in degenerate orbitals can exchange positions. The number of possible exchanges, and so the stabilisation, is greatest for a half-filled or completely filled subshell. Such subshells also have a symmetrical distribution of electrons.
Why: Moving one 4s electron into 3d gives Cr a half-filled 3d⁵ and Cu a full 3d¹⁰ set, and the gain in exchange energy outweighs the small energy difference between 4s and 3d. In oxygen, the fourth 2p electron is paired, and electron–electron repulsion in that orbital makes it easier to remove (IE₁: N 1402 kJ mol⁻¹, O 1314 kJ mol⁻¹).
Why not the others: (A) These are the configurations predicted by the Aufbau order alone; the observed ones differ. (B) Nitrogen's IE₁ is higher, despite its smaller nuclear charge. (D) Half-filled subshells are more stable, not less.
Key point: Half-filled and filled subshells: symmetry and maximum exchange energy give extra stability.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: How the modern periodic law resolves Mendeleev's atomic-mass anomalies, and locating elements 114 and 117 from their configurations
questions.question: Which statement about the modern periodic law is correct?
options: A) Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, so potassium is placed before argon
B) Element 114 belongs to group 4, since 1 + 1 + 4 = 6
C) The modern periodic law is based on the number of neutrons in the nucleus

D) Properties are periodic functions of atomic number, as shown by Moseley's X-ray work; this places argon (39.9 u) before potassium (39.1 u), cobalt before nickel and tellurium before iodine; element 114 ([Rn]5f¹⁴6d¹⁰7s²7p²) falls in group 14 and element 117 (7p⁵) in group 17, both in period 7
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Periodic in atomic number; resolves Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I; Z = 114 is in group 14 and Z = 117 in group 17, period 7.
Concept: Moseley found that the square root of the frequency of characteristic X-rays of elements is proportional to atomic number, not atomic mass. The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. The period number equals the principal quantum number of the outermost shell, and in the p block the group number is 10 + the number of valence (ns + np) electrons.
Why: Mendeleev had to reverse the mass order for pairs such as Te and I to keep elements with similar properties together; ordering by Z removes these anomalies. Element 114 has 7s²7p² (4 valence electrons), so it is in group 10 + 4 = 14; element 117 has 7s²7p⁵, so it is in group 17.
Why not the others: (A) Ordering by mass would place K before Ar, putting a reactive metal among the noble gases. (B) The group follows from the valence configuration, not the digits of Z. (C) Isotopes of one element have different numbers of neutrons but identical positions.
Key point: Periodic law is based on Z; p-block group = 10 + (ns + np electrons); period = outermost n.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linking bond order with bond length and bond enthalpy for C–C bonds, and the equal bonds in benzene and carbonate
questions.question: Typical bond lengths are C–C 154 pm (ethane), C=C 134 pm (ethene) and C≡C 120 pm (ethyne); all C–C bonds in benzene are 139 pm, and all three C–O bonds in CO₃²⁻ are equal. Which statement is correct?
options: A) A higher bond order gives a shorter, stronger bond (bond enthalpies roughly 348, 614 and 839 kJ mol⁻¹ for single, double and triple C–C bonds); resonance makes benzene's bonds equal with bond order 1.5, so their length lies between single and double, and each C–O bond in carbonate has bond order 4/3
B) A higher bond order gives a longer bond
C) Benzene has alternating single and double bonds of 154 and 134 pm
D) In carbonate, one C–O bond is a double bond and is shorter than the other two
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Higher bond order: shorter and stronger; benzene bond order 1.5; carbonate 4/3.
Concept: Bond order is the number of bonding electron pairs shared between two atoms. As bond order increases, bond length decreases and bond enthalpy increases. When a molecule is a resonance hybrid, the bond orders and lengths are averaged over the contributing structures.
Why: Benzene's two Kekulé structures give each C–C bond order (1 + 2)/2 = 1.5, so its length (139 pm) is between 154 and 134 pm. In CO₃²⁻, one double bond is shared over three positions, so each C–O bond has order (2 + 1 + 1)/3 = 4/3, and all three bonds are the same length.
Why not the others: (B) Bond length decreases as bond order rises. (C) X-ray data show all six C–C bonds in benzene are equal. (D) Resonance makes all three C–O bonds identical.
Key point: Bond order up: length down, enthalpy up; resonance averages bond orders.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Applying Fajans' rules to compare the covalent character of halides, including copper(I) chloride, and relating dipole moment to shape
questions.question: Which statement about polarity and covalent character is correct?
options: A) NaCl is more covalent than CuCl, because Na⁺ is smaller than Cu⁺

B) Covalent character increases with a smaller, more highly charged cation, a larger anion and a cation with an 18-electron (pseudo-noble-gas) outer shell; so LiI is more covalent than LiF, AlCl₃ more covalent than NaCl, and CuCl more covalent (lower melting point) than NaCl although Cu⁺ and Na⁺ are similar in size; CO₂ has zero dipole moment because it is linear, while bent H₂O has a dipole moment of about 1.85 D
C) CO₂ has a large dipole moment because each C=O bond is polar
D) Large cations polarise anions more strongly than small cations
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Fajans' rules: small, highly charged or 18-electron cations and large anions increase covalent character; dipole moment depends on shape.
Concept: Fajans' rules: a cation distorts (polarises) the electron cloud of a neighbouring anion. Polarisation, and so covalent character, increases when the cation is small and highly charged, when the anion is large (easily polarised), and when the cation has an 18-electron (n − 1)d¹⁰ outer shell, which shields the nuclear charge poorly. The dipole moment of a molecule is the vector sum of its bond dipoles.
Why: I⁻ is far larger than F⁻, so LiI is more covalent. Al³⁺ is small and triply charged. Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) polarises Cl⁻ more than Na⁺ (2p⁶) does, so CuCl melts much lower than NaCl. In linear O=C=O, the two bond dipoles cancel; in bent H₂O they add.
Why not the others: (A) Cu⁺, with its 18-electron shell, is the more polarising ion. (C) The bond dipoles cancel in a linear molecule. (D) Small cations polarise more strongly.
Key point: Fajans: small, highly charged or 18-electron cation plus large anion means more covalent; net dipole is the vector sum of bond dipoles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: What constant-volume and constant-pressure calorimeters measure, and why Cp exceeds Cv for an ideal gas
questions.question: Which statement about heat capacity and the measurement of ΔU and ΔH is correct?
options: A) A bomb calorimeter measures ΔH directly, because the reaction takes place at constant pressure
B) Cp and Cv are equal for all ideal gases
C) In a constant-pressure (coffee-cup) calorimeter the heat measured is ΔU

D) A bomb calorimeter is a sealed, rigid vessel, so no expansion work is done and the heat measured is q_V = ΔU; a calorimeter open to the atmosphere measures q_P = ΔH; for one mole of an ideal gas Cp − Cv = R, because at constant pressure part of the heat supplied is used to do expansion work; for solids and liquids Cp ≈ Cv
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Bomb (constant V): ΔU; open (constant P): ΔH; Cp − Cv = R for an ideal gas.
Concept: From the first law, ΔU = q + w. At constant volume w = 0 (no PV work), so q_V = ΔU. At constant pressure, q_P = ΔU + PΔV = ΔH. Heat capacity C = q/ΔT; molar heat capacities at constant pressure and volume are Cp and Cv.
Why: For one mole of ideal gas heated by ΔT at constant pressure, the gas also does work PΔV = RΔT, so q_P = CvΔT + RΔT; hence Cp = Cv + R. Solids and liquids expand very little, so the difference is negligible. In a bomb calorimeter, the heat released raises the temperature of the bomb and the surrounding water; multiplying the rise by the calorimeter's heat capacity gives q_V.
Why not the others: (A) The bomb is rigid, so the process is at constant volume, giving ΔU. (B) Cp exceeds Cv by R. (C) Constant pressure gives ΔH.
Key point: q_V = ΔU, q_P = ΔH; Cp − Cv = R (ideal gas).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Enthalpy of formation of ethene from combustion data by Hess's law, then the enthalpy of hydrogenation of ethene
questions.question: Use these standard enthalpies: combustion of C(graphite) −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹; combustion of H₂(g) to H₂O(l) −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹; combustion of C₂H₄(g) −1411.0 kJ mol⁻¹; formation of C₂H₆(g) −84.7 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the standard enthalpy of formation of ethene, and what is the enthalpy of hydrogenation, C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g)?
options: A) −52.4 kJ mol⁻¹; −32.3 kJ mol⁻¹
B) +52.4 kJ mol⁻¹; −137.1 kJ mol⁻¹
C) +52.4 kJ mol⁻¹; +137.1 kJ mol⁻¹
D) −731.4 kJ mol⁻¹; +646.7 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ΔfH(C₂H₄) = +52.4 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔhydH = −137.1 kJ mol⁻¹.
Concept: Hess's law: the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it takes place in one step or several, so enthalpy changes can be added like equations. ΔrH = Σ ΔfH(products) − Σ ΔfH(reactants); the enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is zero.
Given: ΔfH(CO₂) = −393.5; ΔfH(H₂O, l) = −285.8; ΔcH(C₂H₄) = −1411.0; ΔfH(C₂H₆) = −84.7 kJ mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O: ΔcH = 2ΔfH(CO₂) + 2ΔfH(H₂O) − ΔfH(C₂H₄).
Step 1: ΔfH(C₂H₄) = 2(−393.5) + 2(−285.8) − (−1411.0) = −787.0 − 571.6 + 1411.0 = +52.4 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: Hydrogenation: ΔH = ΔfH(C₂H₆) − ΔfH(C₂H₄) − 0 = −84.7 − 52.4 = −137.1 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why: Ethene is slightly endothermic relative to its elements; adding H₂ across the double bond releases heat, as the weaker π bond is replaced by two stronger C–H σ bonds.
Why not the others: (A) Sign error in Step 1 carried through. (C) Hydrogenation of an alkene is exothermic. (D) Adds the combustion enthalpy instead of subtracting it.
Key point: Hess's law: ΔrH = Σ ΔfH(products) − Σ ΔfH(reactants).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Degree of ionisation of formic acid at two concentrations, when the usual approximation fails, and with a common ion present
questions.question: For formic acid, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ at 298 K. What is its degree of ionisation α (i) in a 0.10 M solution and (ii) in a 0.0010 M solution, and (iii) what is α in 0.10 M formic acid that also contains 0.10 M sodium formate?
options: B) (i) 4.2 %; (ii) 42 %, using α = √(Ka/c); (iii) 4.2 %, unchanged by the salt
C) (i) about 4.2 %; (ii) about 34 % (the approximation α ≈ √(Ka/c) fails, so the quadratic must be solved); (iii) about 0.18 %, because the common formate ion suppresses ionisation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4.2 %; about 34 %; about 0.18 %.
Concept: For a weak acid HA of concentration c, Ka = cα²/(1 − α). When α is small, α ≈ √(Ka/c) (Ostwald's dilution law): dilution increases α. If α is not small, the full quadratic must be solved. Adding a salt containing A⁻ shifts the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ to the left (common ion effect).
Given: Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴; c = 0.10 M and 0.0010 M; [HCOO⁻] from salt = 0.10 M.
Formula/Principle: Ka = cα²/(1 − α); with salt, Ka ≈ [H⁺](0.10)/0.10 = cα, so α ≈ Ka/c.
Step 1: (i) α ≈ √(1.8 × 10⁻⁴/0.10) = √(1.8 × 10⁻³) ≈ 0.042 (4.2 %); small, so the approximation holds.
Step 2: (ii) √(1.8 × 10⁻⁴/10⁻³) = 0.42 is not small; solving 10⁻³α² + 1.8 × 10⁻⁴α − 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ = 0 gives α ≈ 0.34.
Step 3: (iii) α ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁴/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻³ (0.18 %).
Why: Dilution favours ionisation because the product side has more particles; added formate ions push the equilibrium back towards un-ionised acid.
Why not the others: (A) Uses Ka/c for the pure acid and reverses the effect of the salt. (B) Applies the approximation where α is large, and ignores the common ion effect. (D) Uses the Ka of acetic acid.
Key point: α ≈ √(Ka/c) only when α is small; a common ion reduces α to about Ka/[A⁻].

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the pH of 0.010 M solutions of a strong acid, weak acid, salts and a strong base
questions.question: Which order of pH, from lowest to highest, is correct for 0.010 M aqueous solutions at 298 K? (Ka of CH₃COOH = Kb of NH₃ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵)
options: A) HCl < CH₃COOH < NH₄Cl < NaCl < CH₃COONa < NaOH (approximately 2.0, 3.4, 5.6, 7.0, 8.4 and 12.0)
B) CH₃COOH < HCl < NaCl < NH₄Cl < NaOH < CH₃COONa
C) HCl < NH₄Cl < CH₃COOH < CH₃COONa < NaCl < NaOH
D) All the salt solutions have pH 7
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) HCl (2.0) < CH₃COOH (3.4) < NH₄Cl (5.6) < NaCl (7.0) < CH₃COONa (8.4) < NaOH (12.0).
Concept: Strong acids and bases ionise completely. A weak acid gives [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka c). A salt of a strong acid and a weak base (NH₄Cl) is acidic by hydrolysis; a salt of a weak acid and a strong base (CH₃COONa) is basic; a salt of a strong acid and a strong base (NaCl) is neutral.
Why: HCl: pH = 2.0. CH₃COOH: [H⁺] = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4.2 × 10⁻⁴, pH ≈ 3.4. NH₄Cl: Kh = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰; [H⁺] = √(5.6 × 10⁻¹²) ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻⁶, pH ≈ 5.6. CH₃COONa: by the same calculation [OH⁻] ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻⁶, pH ≈ 8.4. NaOH: pOH = 2, pH = 12.
Why not the others: (B) A strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid at the same concentration, and NaOH has the highest pH. (C) The weak acid is more acidic than the hydrolysed salt NH₄Cl, and NaCl is neutral. (D) Salts of weak acids or weak bases hydrolyse.
Key point: Strong acid < weak acid < acidic salt < neutral salt < basic salt < strong base.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Percentage of nitrogen by Kjeldahl's method and of chlorine by Carius method, and the limits of Kjeldahl's method
questions.question: (i) In Kjeldahl's method, 0.30 g of an organic compound is digested, and the ammonia evolved exactly neutralises 10.0 mL of 0.50 M H₂SO₄. (ii) In Carius method, 0.20 g of another compound gives 0.287 g of AgCl. What are the percentages of nitrogen and chlorine? (N = 14, Ag = 108, Cl = 35.5)
options: A) 46.7 % N; 35.5 % Cl; Kjeldahl's method cannot be used for compounds with nitrogen in nitro or azo groups or in a ring (as in pyridine), because this nitrogen is not converted to ammonium sulphate
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 46.7 % N; 35.5 % Cl.
Concept: In Kjeldahl's method, the nitrogen of the compound is converted to ammonium sulphate by heating with concentrated H₂SO₄; the ammonia released by alkali is absorbed in a known amount of standard acid. In Carius method, the compound is heated with fuming HNO₃ and AgNO₃, and the halogen is weighed as silver halide.
Given: 10.0 mL of 0.50 M H₂SO₄; mass 0.30 g; 0.287 g AgCl from 0.20 g.
Formula/Principle: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄; % N = (moles NH₃ × 14 ÷ mass) × 100; % Cl = (35.5/143.5) × (mass AgCl ÷ mass) × 100.
Step 1: Moles H₂SO₄ = 5.0 × 10⁻³; moles NH₃ = 1.0 × 10⁻²; mass N = 0.140 g; % N = 0.140/0.30 × 100 = 46.7 % (as in urea).
Step 2: % Cl = (35.5/143.5) × (0.287/0.20) × 100 = 35.5 %.
Why: Each H₂SO₄ neutralises two NH₃, so the moles of N are twice the moles of acid. Nitrogen in nitro and azo groups and in pyridine rings is not converted to ammonium sulphate.
Why not the others: (B) Forgets that each H₂SO₄ takes two NH₃. (C) Uses 71 (Cl₂) instead of 35.5 for Cl. (D) Counts four NH₃ per H₂SO₄, and halves the chlorine.
Key point: Kjeldahl: moles N = 2 × moles H₂SO₄; Carius: % X from mass of AgX.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Working out alkene structures from ozonolysis products and predicting the products of hot permanganate oxidation
questions.question: Two alkenes P and Q both have the formula C₆H₁₂. On ozonolysis (O₃, then Zn/H₂O), P gives propanone as the only product, while Q gives ethanal and butan-2-one. What are P and Q, and what does Q give with hot acidified KMnO₄?
options: A) P is hex-3-ene and Q is hex-2-ene; Q gives ethanoic acid and butanoic acid
B) P is 2-methylpent-2-ene and Q is 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene
C) P is 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene and Q is 3-methylpent-2-ene; with hot acidified KMnO₄, Q gives ethanoic acid and butan-2-one
D) P is 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene and Q is 3-methylpent-2-ene; with hot KMnO₄, Q gives ethanal and butanal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P = 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene; Q = 3-methylpent-2-ene; Q gives ethanoic acid and butan-2-one.
Concept: Reductive ozonolysis splits a C=C bond, turning each double-bond carbon into C=O: a carbon with H gives an aldehyde; a carbon with two alkyl groups gives a ketone. Hot acidified KMnO₄ also cleaves the double bond, but oxidises any aldehyde formed to a carboxylic acid; ketones are not oxidised further.
Why: A single product, propanone (CH₃)₂C=O, means both ends were (CH₃)₂C=, so P is (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂. Joining ethanal (CH₃CH=) and butan-2-one (=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃) gives CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, 3-methylpent-2-ene (2 + 4 = 6 carbons). With KMnO₄, the CH₃CH= end becomes CH₃COOH.
Why not the others: (A) Hex-3-ene would give only propanal, and hex-2-ene ethanal plus butanal. (B) 2-Methylpent-2-ene gives propanone and propanal. (D) Hot KMnO₄ oxidises aldehydes to acids; butanal does not arise from this structure.
Key point: Ozonolysis: =CH– gives aldehyde, =CR₂ gives ketone; hot KMnO₄ turns the aldehyde into an acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Acidity of terminal alkynes explained by hybridisation, and Markovnikov hydration of propyne
questions.question: Which statement about alkynes is correct?
options: A) All alkynes, including but-2-yne, react with sodamide to give sodium alkynides
B) Ethene is more acidic than ethyne, because it has more hydrogen atoms
C) Hydration of propyne with dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄ gives propanal

D) Ethyne and propyne react with sodium or sodamide, liberating hydrogen or ammonia and forming alkynides, because a hydrogen on an sp carbon (50 % s character, more electronegative) is weakly acidic; but-2-yne has no such hydrogen; so the acidity order is HC≡CH > H₂C=CH₂ > CH₃–CH₃; propyne adds water (HgSO₄, dilute H₂SO₄, 333 K) through an enol to give propanone
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic (sp carbon); but-2-yne is not; propyne hydrates to propanone.
Concept: The greater the s character of a hybrid orbital, the closer its electrons are held to the nucleus, so the carbon becomes more electronegative and the C–H bond more polar. sp carbons (50 % s) are more electronegative than sp² (33 %) and sp³ (25 %) carbons. Addition of water to an alkyne follows Markovnikov's rule; the enol formed tautomerises to the carbonyl compound.
Why: HC≡CH + Na → HC≡C⁻Na⁺ + ½H₂. The C–H bond in ethene and ethane does not react this way. In propyne, OH adds to C-2, giving CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which rearranges to CH₃COCH₃.
Why not the others: (A) But-2-yne, CH₃C≡CCH₃, has no hydrogen on an sp carbon. (B) More hydrogens do not mean more acidity; the hybridisation of carbon matters. (C) Markovnikov addition puts the oxygen on the inner carbon, giving a ketone.
Key point: Acidity of C–H: sp > sp² > sp³; terminal alkynes form alkynides; hydration gives ketones (except ethyne gives ethanal).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Van't Hoff factor and degree of dissociation of a salt MX₂ from freezing point, and degree of association of acetic acid in benzene
questions.question: (i) A 0.10 mol kg⁻¹ aqueous solution of a salt MX₂ freezes at −0.465 °C (Kf of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹). (ii) 1.2 g of acetic acid in 100 g of benzene lowers the freezing point by 0.60 K (Kf of benzene = 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹; true molar mass 60 g mol⁻¹). What is the degree of dissociation of MX₂, and what is the degree of association (dimerisation) of acetic acid?
options: B) 0.75; about 0.83, from an apparent molar mass of about 102 g mol⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) MX₂: α = 0.75; acetic acid: degree of association ≈ 0.83.
Concept: The van't Hoff factor i = observed colligative property ÷ value expected with no dissociation or association. For dissociation into n ions, i = 1 + (n − 1)α. For association into dimers, i = 1 − α/2. The apparent molar mass from a colligative measurement is the true molar mass ÷ i.
Given: ΔTf = 0.465 K, m = 0.10, Kf = 1.86; acetic acid: w = 1.2 g, W = 100 g, ΔTf = 0.60 K, Kf = 5.12.
Formula/Principle: ΔTf = iKf m; M_apparent = 1000 Kf w/(ΔTf W).
Step 1: MX₂: i = 0.465/(1.86 × 0.10) = 2.5; n = 3, so 2.5 = 1 + 2α, α = 0.75.
Step 2: Acetic acid: M_apparent = 1000 × 5.12 × 1.2/(0.60 × 100) = 102.4 g mol⁻¹; i = 60/102.4 = 0.586.
Step 3: 0.586 = 1 − α/2, so α = 0.83.
Why: Salts dissociate in water, raising the number of particles; acetic acid forms hydrogen-bonded dimers in benzene, lowering it, so its apparent molar mass is close to twice the true value.
Why not the others: (A) Uses n = 4 for MX₂ and the wrong association formula. (C) Gets MX₂ right but uses i = 1 − α for the dimer. (D) Gives the van't Hoff factor of MX₂ and a meaningless degree of association, which cannot exceed 1.
Key point: Dissociation: i = 1 + (n − 1)α; dimerisation: i = 1 − α/2; M_apparent = M/i.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading the dependence of the emf of a Daniell cell on zinc-ion concentration and predicting a new emf with the Nernst equation
questions.question:
The emf of the cell Zn | Zn²⁺(c) || Cu²⁺(1.0 M) | Cu was measured at 298 K for different values of c.
| [Zn²⁺] / M | 1.0 | 0.10 | 0.010 |
|---|---|---|---|
| E / V | 1.100 | 1.130 | 1.159 |
What does the trend show, and what emf is expected when [Zn²⁺] = 1.0 M and [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 M?
options: A) E rises by 0.059 V for every tenfold decrease in [Zn²⁺]; expected emf 1.159 V
B) E rises by about 0.0295 V for every tenfold decrease in [Zn²⁺], as given by E = E° − (0.059/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]); expected emf about 1.041 V
C) E does not depend on concentration; expected emf 1.100 V
D) E falls as [Zn²⁺] decreases; expected emf 1.159 V
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) E changes by 0.0295 V per tenfold change; the expected emf is about 1.041 V.
Concept: For Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu (n = 2), the Nernst equation at 298 K is E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q, with Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]. Reducing the product concentration or raising the reactant concentration increases E.
Given: E° = 1.100 V; data at [Cu²⁺] = 1.0 M; new conditions [Zn²⁺] = 1.0 M, [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 M.
Formula/Principle: E = 1.100 − 0.0295 log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]).
Step 1: From the table: 1.130 − 1.100 = 0.030 V and 1.159 − 1.130 ≈ 0.029 V per decade, matching 0.059/2.
Step 2: New Q = 1.0/0.010 = 100; E = 1.100 − 0.0295 × 2 = 1.041 V.
Why: Lowering [Cu²⁺] makes the cathode reaction less favourable, so the emf falls; lowering [Zn²⁺] has the opposite effect.
Why not the others: (A) The slope is 0.059/n with n = 2, and decreasing [Cu²⁺] lowers the emf. (C) The table shows a clear dependence on concentration. (D) E rises, not falls, as [Zn²⁺] decreases.
Key point: E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q; n = 2 gives 0.0295 V per decade.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Following a first-order gas-phase decomposition by the rise in total pressure, and finding the half-life and later total pressure
questions.question: The gas-phase reaction A(g) → B(g) + C(g) is first order. Starting with pure A at 0.40 atm in a rigid vessel at constant temperature, the total pressure is 0.60 atm after 10 min. What are the half-life and the rate constant, and what will the total pressure be after 30 min?
options: A) 10 min; 0.0693 min⁻¹; 0.75 atm
B) 20 min; 0.0347 min⁻¹; 0.70 atm
C) 10 min; 0.0693 min⁻¹; 0.80 atm
D) 5 min; 0.139 min⁻¹; 0.80 atm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) t½ = 10 min; k = 0.0693 min⁻¹; 0.75 atm.
Concept: For A → B + C, if the pressure of A falls by x, the total pressure is (P₀ − x) + x + x = P₀ + x, so P_A = 2P₀ − P_total. For a first-order reaction, k = (2.303/t) log(P₀/P_A), and t½ = 0.693/k does not depend on the starting pressure.
Given: P₀ = 0.40 atm; P_total = 0.60 atm at 10 min.
Formula/Principle: P_A = 2P₀ − P_total; t½ = 0.693/k.
Step 1: At 10 min: P_A = 0.80 − 0.60 = 0.20 atm = P₀/2, so t½ = 10 min and k = 0.693/10 = 0.0693 min⁻¹.
Step 2: 30 min is three half-lives: P_A = 0.40/8 = 0.050 atm.
Step 3: P_total = 2P₀ − P_A = 0.80 − 0.050 = 0.75 atm.
Why: Each molecule of A that reacts gives two molecules, so the total pressure rises towards 2P₀ = 0.80 atm but approaches it only slowly.
Why not the others: (B) Treats the rise in total pressure (0.20 atm) as the fall in P_A over two half-lives. (C) Assumes the reaction is complete by 30 min. (D) Takes the time for the total pressure to rise by 0.10 atm as the half-life.
Key point: A → B + C: P_A = 2P₀ − P_total; first order has a constant half-life.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: How transition metals act as catalysts, and the nature of interstitial compounds and alloys
questions.question: Which statement about the catalytic properties, interstitial compounds and alloys of transition metals is correct?
options: A) Transition metals are good catalysts because they have only one oxidation state
B) Interstitial compounds such as TiC and Fe₃H are soft, low-melting ionic solids with fixed formulas

C) Transition metals and their compounds catalyse reactions by providing surfaces for adsorption (Fe in the Haber process, Ni in hydrogenation, V₂O₅ in the contact process) and by changing oxidation state, as in the Fe³⁺-catalysed reaction of I⁻ with S₂O₈²⁻; interstitial compounds, formed when small atoms such as H, C or N occupy voids in the metal lattice, are hard, high-melting, non-stoichiometric and keep metallic conductivity; alloys form readily because the atomic radii of transition metals differ by less than about 15 %
D) Alloys can form only between metals with very different atomic radii
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Adsorption and variable oxidation states explain catalysis; interstitial compounds are hard, high-melting and non-stoichiometric; similar radii allow alloys.
Concept: Transition metals have several oxidation states and can form complexes, and their surfaces can adsorb reactant molecules, weakening bonds and increasing local concentration. Interstitial compounds (TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H, TiH₁.₇) have small atoms trapped in the holes of the metal lattice. Alloys are blends of metals; transition metals readily replace one another in a lattice because their sizes are similar.
Why: Fe³⁺ catalysis: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, then 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻; the catalyst is regenerated. Interstitial compounds have higher melting points than the pure metals, are very hard and chemically inert, and conduct electricity. Brass (Cu–Zn) and steels are examples of alloys.
Why not the others: (A) Variable oxidation states are part of what makes them good catalysts. (B) Interstitial compounds are hard, high-melting and non-stoichiometric. (D) Similar atomic radii favour alloy formation.
Key point: Catalysis: adsorption + variable oxidation states; interstitial compounds: hard, high mp, non-stoichiometric; alloys: similar radii.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Complexes in the cyanide extraction of gold and in photographic fixing, with the oxidation states and coordination numbers of the metals
questions.question: Gold is extracted by the reactions 4Au + 8CN⁻ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4[Au(CN)₂]⁻ + 4OH⁻ and 2[Au(CN)₂]⁻ + Zn → [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻ + 2Au. In photography, unexposed silver bromide is removed by AgBr + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻ + Br⁻. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Gold is reduced by cyanide in the first step, and its oxidation state in [Au(CN)₂]⁻ is −1
B) Zinc is oxidised in the second step and forms an octahedral complex
C) Silver bromide dissolves in hypo because Ag⁺ is reduced to silver metal

D) In the first step gold is oxidised by O₂ from 0 to +1 and held in solution as [Au(CN)₂]⁻ (coordination number 2); in the second step Zn displaces gold and becomes Zn(II) in [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻ (coordination number 4); in fixing, insoluble AgBr dissolves by forming the soluble complex [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻, in which silver is +1 with coordination number 2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Au 0 → +1 in [Au(CN)₂]⁻ (CN = 2); Zn → +2 in [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻ (CN = 4); Ag stays +1 in [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻ (CN = 2).
Concept: Forming a stable complex can pull a metal or an insoluble salt into solution. In metallurgy, gold and silver are leached with dilute cyanide in air, then recovered by displacement with a more reactive metal, zinc. In photography, sodium thiosulphate (hypo) dissolves unexposed AgBr as a thiosulphato complex.
Why: Oxidation state of Au in [Au(CN)₂]⁻: x + 2(−1) = −1, so x = +1. Zn: x + 4(−1) = −2, so x = +2. Ag: x + 2(−2) = −3, so x = +1. In fixing, no redox occurs; complex formation alone removes Ag⁺ from the solid.
Why not the others: (A) Gold is oxidised by O₂, to +1. (B) [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻ is a four-coordinate complex. (C) Ag⁺ stays +1; dissolution is due to complex formation.
Key point: Cyanide leaching: Au → [Au(CN)₂]⁻, recovered with Zn; hypo dissolves AgBr as [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting pKa values of ethanol and substituted phenols in terms of resonance and electron-withdrawing or -donating groups
questions.question:
The table gives pKa values in water at 298 K.
| Compound | pKa |
|---|---|
| Ethanol | 15.9 |
| 4-Methylphenol | 10.2 |
| Phenol | 10.0 |
| 4-Chlorophenol | 9.4 |
| 3-Nitrophenol | 8.4 |
| 4-Nitrophenol | 7.1 |
Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) Phenol is far more acidic than ethanol because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of its charge into the ring; electron-withdrawing groups (Cl, NO₂) increase acidity and electron-donating CH₃ decreases it; a nitro group at the para position is more effective than at meta, because it can withdraw electrons by resonance only from the ortho and para positions
B) Ethanol is more acidic than phenol
C) A methyl group increases the acidity of phenol
D) The nitro group has the same effect whether it is at the meta or the para position
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Resonance-stabilised phenoxide; EWG raise acidity, EDG lower it; para-NO₂ beats meta-NO₂.
Concept: A lower pKa means a stronger acid. The acidity of an O–H compound depends on the stability of its anion. In phenoxide, the negative charge is delocalised over the ring; in ethoxide it is localised on oxygen. Substituents that withdraw electrons (−I, −R) spread the charge further and increase acidity; electron-donating groups (+I) do the opposite.
Why: Phenol (10.0) is about 10⁶ times more acidic than ethanol (15.9). CH₃ (+I) raises the pKa to 10.2. Cl (−I) lowers it to 9.4. NO₂ at the para position withdraws by both −I and −R (the charge can reach the nitro group), giving 7.1; at the meta position only the −I effect operates, giving 8.4.
Why not the others: (B) Ethanol's pKa is much higher. (C) CH₃ raises the pKa, so it lowers acidity. (D) The data show a clear difference between meta and para.
Key point: Phenoxide resonance makes phenol acidic; −R groups at o/p increase acidity most.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Temperature-controlled sulphonation of phenol and its use as the first step in a good-yield preparation of picric acid
questions.question: Phenol is treated with concentrated sulphuric acid at about 290 K in one experiment and at about 373 K in another. Separately, picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) is prepared by first sulphonating phenol to phenol-2,4-disulphonic acid and then treating it with concentrated nitric acid. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Sulphonation of phenol gives the meta product at both temperatures
B) Direct nitration of phenol with concentrated HNO₃ gives picric acid in high yield, because phenol is not oxidised
C) The –OH group deactivates the ring, so phenol does not undergo sulphonation

D) The –OH group activates the ring and directs ortho/para: at low temperature the ortho-hydroxybenzenesulphonic acid is the main product, at higher temperature the para isomer; direct nitration with concentrated HNO₃ gives a poor yield of picric acid because phenol is partly oxidised, so phenol is first sulphonated and the –SO₃H groups are then replaced by –NO₂ groups
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) o-Sulphonic acid at low temperature, p-isomer at high temperature; sulphonation then nitration gives picric acid in good yield.
Concept: The –OH group donates electrons to the ring by resonance (+R), so phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution readily at the ortho and para positions. Sulphonation is reversible, so the product depends on temperature: the ortho isomer forms faster, while the para isomer is more stable. Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent, and phenol, an electron-rich ring, is easily oxidised by it.
Why: At about 290 K the faster-forming ortho acid dominates; at about 373 K the reaction reaches equilibrium and the more stable para acid dominates. In the two-step route, the sulphonic acid groups make the ring less easily oxidised; they are then replaced by nitro groups (ipso substitution), giving 2,4,6-trinitrophenol in good yield.
Why not the others: (A) –OH is an ortho/para director. (B) Concentrated HNO₃ oxidises much of the phenol, so the yield is poor. (C) –OH is strongly activating.
Key point: Phenol: o/p director; sulphonation is temperature dependent; picric acid via sulphonation then nitration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Distinguishing pentan-2-one from pentan-3-one and benzaldehyde from acetophenone, and reducing the ketones to the alkane
questions.question: Which statement about distinguishing and reducing carbonyl compounds is correct?
options: A) Pentan-3-one gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform, while pentan-2-one does not
B) Benzaldehyde gives a red precipitate with Fehling's solution

C) Pentan-2-one (a methyl ketone, CH₃CO–) gives iodoform with I₂ and NaOH, while pentan-3-one does not; benzaldehyde gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent, while acetophenone does not (but acetophenone gives iodoform); both pentanones are reduced to pentane by Zn–Hg and concentrated HCl (Clemmensen) or by hydrazine and KOH in ethylene glycol (Wolff–Kishner)
D) Clemmensen reduction converts both pentanones into pentan-2-ol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Iodoform separates the pentanones; Tollens' separates benzaldehyde from acetophenone; Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner gives pentane.
Concept: The iodoform test (I₂/NaOH, yellow CHI₃) is given by compounds with a CH₃CO– group (and by alcohols that oxidise to them). Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO₃) oxidises aldehydes, giving a silver mirror; ketones do not react. Fehling's solution is reduced by aliphatic aldehydes but not by aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde. Clemmensen and Wolff–Kishner reductions convert C=O into CH₂.
Why: Pentan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, has the CH₃CO– group; pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃, does not. Acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃, is a methyl ketone, so it gives iodoform but not a silver mirror. Both pentanones have five carbons in an unbranched chain, so reducing C=O to CH₂ gives pentane in each case.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses the iodoform result. (B) Aromatic aldehydes do not reduce Fehling's solution. (D) These reductions remove the oxygen completely, giving an alkane, not an alcohol.
Key point: Iodoform for CH₃CO–; Tollens' for aldehydes; Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner: C=O → CH₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: How the number, electronegativity and position of electron-withdrawing substituents change the acidity of carboxylic acids
questions.question: Which statement about the acidity of carboxylic acids is correct?
options: A) Acetic acid is a stronger acid than trichloroacetic acid

B) Acidity increases with the number and electronegativity of electron-withdrawing groups near the –COOH group, so CF₃COOH (pKa 0.23) > CCl₃COOH (0.64) > CHCl₂COOH (1.26) > CH₂ClCOOH (2.87) > HCOOH (3.75) > C₆H₅COOH (4.19) > CH₃COOH (4.76); the effect falls off with distance, so 2-chlorobutanoic acid is much stronger than 4-chlorobutanoic acid
C) The position of a chlorine atom in the chain does not affect acidity
D) Electron-donating groups such as –CH₃ make carboxylic acids stronger
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) More, and more electronegative, −I groups close to –COOH increase acidity; the effect decreases with distance.
Concept: Electron-withdrawing groups (−I) stabilise the carboxylate anion by spreading its negative charge, so the acid ionises more. Electron-donating groups (+I) destabilise the anion and decrease acidity. The inductive effect weakens rapidly along a chain of σ bonds.
Why: F is more electronegative than Cl, so CF₃COOH is the strongest; each extra Cl increases acidity. HCOOH, with no alkyl group, is stronger than CH₃COOH, which has a +I methyl group; the sp² phenyl group makes benzoic acid stronger than acetic acid. Cl on C-2 (pKa about 2.9) is next to the carboxyl group; on C-4 (about 4.5) its effect has mostly died away.
Why not the others: (A) Three −I chlorine atoms make trichloroacetic acid much stronger. (C) The inductive effect depends strongly on distance. (D) +I groups weaken carboxylic acids.
Key point: −I groups (more, stronger, closer) increase acidity of carboxylic acids.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: The other end and length of a focal chord of y² = 12x, compared with the latus rectum as the shortest focal chord
questions.question: For the parabola \(y^2=12x\), a focal chord has one end at \((27,18)\). What is its other end, what is its length, and how does it compare with the latus rectum?
options: A) \(\left(\tfrac13,-2\right)\); \(\tfrac{100}3\); longer than the latus rectum (length 12), which is the shortest focal chord
B) \((3,-6)\); 12; equal to the latus rectum
C) \(\left(\tfrac13,2\right)\); \(\tfrac{80}3\); shorter than the latus rectum
D) \((-27,-18)\); \(60\); the latus rectum is the longest focal chord
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\left(\tfrac13,-2\right)\); \(\tfrac{100}3\); the latus rectum (12) is the shortest focal chord.
Given: \(y^2=4ax,\ a=3;\ \text{point }(at^2,2at)=(27,18)\Rightarrow t=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{ends of a focal chord: }t_1t_2=-1;\ \text{length}=a\left(t+\tfrac1t\right)^2\)
Step 1: \(t_2=-\tfrac13\Rightarrow\left(3\cdot\tfrac19,\ 6\cdot\left(-\tfrac13\right)\right)=\left(\tfrac13,-2\right)\)
Step 2: \(\text{length}=3\left(3+\tfrac13\right)^2=3\cdot\tfrac{100}9=\tfrac{100}3\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{focal distances: }(27+3)+\left(\tfrac13+3\right)=\tfrac{100}3;\qquad a\left(t+\tfrac1t\right)^2\ge a(2)^2=4a=12\ \text{at }t=1\]
Check: \[\sqrt{\left(\tfrac{80}3\right)^2+20^2}=\sqrt{\tfrac{6400+3600}9}=\tfrac{100}3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(t+\tfrac1t\ge2\text{ for }t>0\text{, so the length is least when }t=1\text{, the latus rectum }x=a\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{these are the latus-rectum ends, not the other end of this chord}\); (C) \(\text{sign error in the y-coordinate, which puts the point off the line through the focus}\); (D) \((-27,-18)\text{ is not on the parabola (x must be }\ge0)\).
Key point: \(\text{focal chord: }t_1t_2=-1;\ \text{length }a(t+1/t)^2\ge4a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
