questions.sub_topic: Two trigonometric limits needing more than sin x / x → 1: (tan x − sin x)/x³ and cos x/(π/2 − x)
questions.question: What are \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x-\sin x}{x^3}\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\pi/2}\frac{\cos x}{\frac\pi2-x}\)?
options: B) \(\tfrac12\) and \(1\)
C) \(\tfrac12\) and \(0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\tfrac12\) and \(1\).
Given: \(\displaystyle\lim_{\theta\to0}\frac{\sin\theta}\theta=1,\ \lim_{\theta\to0}\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta^2}=\frac12\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tan x-\sin x=\tan x\,(1-\cos x);\ \text{substitute }h=\tfrac\pi2-x\text{ in the second limit}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{\tan x(1-\cos x)}{x^3}=\dfrac{\tan x}{x}\cdot\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x^2}\to1\cdot\tfrac12\)
Step 2: \(\cos x=\cos\left(\tfrac\pi2-h\right)=\sin h\Rightarrow\dfrac{\sin h}{h}\to1\text{ as }h\to0\)
Worked derivation: \[\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x-\sin x}{x^3}=\frac12,\qquad\lim_{x\to\pi/2}\frac{\cos x}{\frac\pi2-x}=1\]
Check: \[x=0.1:\ \frac{0.100335-0.099833}{0.001}=0.502\approx\tfrac12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{splitting }\tan x-\sin x\text{ into a product shows the numerator is of order }x^3\text{, not zero to that order}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{treats }\tan x\approx\sin x\approx x\text{ so the numerator vanishes, an error at order }x^3\); (C) \(\text{the second limit is a }0/0\text{ form equal to 1}\); (D) \(\text{wrong constants and a sign error in the substitution}\).
Key point: \(\tan x-\sin x=\tan x(1-\cos x)\sim x^3/2;\ \text{shift to }h\to0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Mean deviation about the mean and range of a data set, and how both change under y = 5 − 2x
questions.question: For the observations 3, 7, 8, 10 and 12, what is the mean deviation about the mean? If each observation x is replaced by \(y=5-2x\), what are the new mean deviation and range?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.4; 4.8; 18.
Given: \(x:3,7,8,10,12;\ n=5\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{MD}=\dfrac1n\sum|x_i-\bar x|;\ y=a+bx\Rightarrow\text{MD}_y=|b|\,\text{MD}_x,\ \text{range}_y=|b|\,\text{range}_x\)
Step 1: \(\bar x=\dfrac{40}5=8;\ |x_i-8|:5,1,0,2,4;\ \text{sum}=12\Rightarrow\text{MD}=2.4\)
Step 2: \(b=-2\Rightarrow\text{MD}_y=2\times2.4=4.8\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{range}_x=12-3=9\Rightarrow\text{range}_y=|{-2}|\times9=18\]
Check: \[y:-1,-9,-11,-15,-19;\ \bar y=-11;\ |y-\bar y|:10,2,0,4,8\Rightarrow\text{MD}=\tfrac{24}5=4.8\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{adding a constant shifts all values equally; multiplying by b stretches all distances by }|b|\text{, whatever its sign}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{measures of spread cannot be negative}\); (B) \(\text{miscounts one deviation}\); (D) \(\text{forgets to scale the range}\).
Key point: \(y=a+bx:\ \text{MD and range multiply by }|b|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: How P(A ∪ B) and P(exactly one) vary with P(B) for independent events when P(A) = 1/2
questions.question: Events A and B are independent, with \(P(A)=\tfrac12\) and \(P(B)=p\), where \(0\le p\le1\). How do \(P(A\cup B)\) and \(P(\text{exactly one of }A,B)\) depend on p?
options: A) Both equal \(\tfrac12+p\)
B) \(P(A\cup B)=\tfrac12+p\); \(P(\text{exactly one})=p\)
C) \(P(A\cup B)=\tfrac12+\tfrac p2\); \(P(\text{exactly one})=\tfrac p2\)
D) \(P(A\cup B)=\tfrac12+\tfrac p2\), increasing linearly from \(\tfrac12\) to 1; \(P(\text{exactly one})=\tfrac12\) for every p
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(P(A\cup B)=\tfrac12+\tfrac p2\); \(P(\text{exactly one})=\tfrac12\) for all p.
Given: \(P(A)=\tfrac12,\ P(B)=p;\ \text{independent}\Rightarrow P(A\cap B)=\tfrac p2\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B);\ P(\text{exactly one})=P(A)+P(B)-2P(A\cap B)\)
Step 1: \(P(A\cup B)=\tfrac12+p-\tfrac p2=\tfrac12+\tfrac p2\)
Step 2: \(P(\text{exactly one})=\tfrac12+p-p=\tfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[P(A\cap B^c)+P(A^c\cap B)=\tfrac12(1-p)+\tfrac12p=\tfrac12\]
Check: \[p=0:\ P(A\cup B)=\tfrac12=P(A)\ \checkmark;\quad p=1:\ P(A\cup B)=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{with }P(A)=\tfrac12\text{, whatever happens with B, exactly one occurs precisely when A's outcome differs from B's, which has probability }\tfrac12\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the overlap and can exceed 1}\); (B) \(\text{forgets to subtract }P(A\cap B)\); (C) \(\text{the union is right but exactly-one is not }p/2\).
Key point: \(\text{independent: }P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the unknown number of red balls in one urn from the overall probability of red, then the reverse (Bayes) probability
questions.question: Urn I has 3 red and 2 black balls; urn II has x red and 2 black balls. A fair coin decides the urn, and one ball is drawn. If the probability of drawing a red ball is \(\tfrac7{10}\), what is x, and given that the ball drawn is red, what is the probability it came from urn I?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(x=8;\ \tfrac37\).
Given: \(P(E_1)=P(E_2)=\tfrac12;\ P(R\mid E_1)=\tfrac35,\ P(R\mid E_2)=\tfrac{x}{x+2};\ P(R)=\tfrac7{10}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{total probability: }P(R)=\sum P(E_i)P(R\mid E_i);\ \text{Bayes: }P(E_1\mid R)=\dfrac{P(E_1)P(R\mid E_1)}{P(R)}\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac35+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{x}{x+2}=\tfrac7{10}\Rightarrow\tfrac{x}{x+2}=\tfrac45\)
Step 2: \(5x=4x+8\Rightarrow x=8\)
Worked derivation: \[P(E_1\mid R)=\frac{\frac12\cdot\frac35}{\frac7{10}}=\frac{3/10}{7/10}=\frac37\]
Check: \[\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac35+\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac8{10}=0.3+0.4=0.7\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the overall probability is a weighted average of the urn probabilities, so it fixes the unknown urn's probability}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=4\text{ gives }P(R)=\tfrac{19}{30}\); (B) \(x=6\text{ gives }P(R)=\tfrac{27}{40}\); (D) \(\tfrac35\text{ is }P(R\mid E_1)\text{, not }P(E_1\mid R)\).
Key point: \(P(R)=\sum P(E_i)P(R\mid E_i);\ \text{then Bayes reverses it}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding unknown entries of a 3 × 3 matrix from the cofactors of its first row and its determinant
questions.question: A \(3\times3\) matrix has first row \((a,1,4)\) and second row \((1,b,2)\). The cofactors of the elements of its first row are \(2,-3\) and \(1\), and its determinant is 5. What are a and b?
options: D) \(a=\tfrac52,\ b=-\tfrac43\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(a=2,\ b=\tfrac43\).
Given: \(C_{11}=2,\ C_{12}=-3,\ C_{13}=1;\ \det=5\)
Formula/Principle: \(\det=a_{11}C_{11}+a_{12}C_{12}+a_{13}C_{13};\ \text{elements of one row times cofactors of a different row sum to }0\)
Step 1: \(2a+1(-3)+4(1)=5\Rightarrow2a+1=5\Rightarrow a=2\)
Step 2: \(1(2)+b(-3)+2(1)=0\Rightarrow4-3b=0\)
Worked derivation: \[b=\tfrac43\]
Check: \[\text{row 2 with row-1 cofactors is the determinant of a matrix with two equal rows, so it must be }0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{replacing row 1 by row 2 and expanding along row 1 gives a determinant with two identical rows}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{sets the row-2 expansion equal to the determinant instead of 0}\); (C) \(\text{solves }a+1=2\text{ by dropping the cofactor 2}\); (D) \(\text{uses }+3\text{ for }C_{12}\).
Key point: \(\sum_ja_{ij}C_{kj}=\det\text{ if }i=k,\ 0\text{ if }i\ne k\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Area of a triangle by determinants as a function of one coordinate, and the collinear case
questions.question: For the points \(P(1,2),\ Q(3,k),\ R(5,6)\), for which k are they collinear, and for which k is the area of triangle PQR equal to 8?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(k=4\); \(k=0\) or \(k=8\).
Given: \(P(1,2),\ Q(3,k),\ R(5,6)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{area}=\tfrac12\left|\begin{vmatrix}1&2&1\\3&k&1\\5&6&1\end{vmatrix}\right|\)
Step 1: \(\text{determinant}=1(k-6)-2(3-5)+1(18-5k)=k-6+4+18-5k=16-4k\)
Step 2: \(\text{area}=\tfrac12|16-4k|=|8-2k|;\ \text{collinear}\iff k=4\)
Worked derivation: \[|8-2k|=8\Rightarrow k=0\text{ or }k=8\]
Check: \[k=4:\ Q=(3,4)\text{ is the midpoint of PR}\ \checkmark;\quad k=0:\ \tfrac12|16|=8\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the area is zero exactly when the three points lie on one line; the modulus gives two positions of Q, one on each side of PR}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgets the absolute value, missing }k=8\); (B) \(\text{sign error in the collinear value}\); (C) \(\text{miscomputes the determinant}\).
Key point: \(\text{area}=\tfrac12|\det|;\ \text{zero means collinear; the modulus gives two solutions}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Values of k for which y = x^k satisfies a second-order equation, and a combination of the solutions
questions.question: For which values of k does \(y=x^k\ (x>0)\) satisfy \(x^2y''-4xy'+6y=0\)? Does \(y=2x^2-x^3\) also satisfy it?
options: C) \(k=2,3\); no, because a combination of solutions is never a solution
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(k=2,3\); yes.
Given: \(y=x^k,\ y'=kx^{k-1},\ y''=k(k-1)x^{k-2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{substitute and divide by }x^k\)
Step 1: \(k(k-1)x^k-4kx^k+6x^k=0\Rightarrow k^2-5k+6=0\)
Step 2: \((k-2)(k-3)=0\Rightarrow k=2,3\)
Worked derivation: \[y=2x^2-x^3:\ y'=4x-3x^2,\ y''=4-6x;\ x^2(4-6x)-4x(4x-3x^2)+6(2x^2-x^3)=(4-16+12)x^2+(-6+12-6)x^3=0\]
Check: \[k=2:\ 2-8+6=0\ \checkmark;\ k=3:\ 6-12+6=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the equation is linear in y, so any combination }c_1x^2+c_2x^3\text{ is also a solution}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{solves }k^2-7k+6=0\text{ (sign slip)}\); (C) \(\text{for a linear equation, combinations of solutions are solutions}\); (D) \(\text{signs of the roots reversed}\).
Key point: \(\text{try }y=x^k;\ \text{linear equations allow combinations of solutions}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Points of discontinuity of f(x) = [x] + [−x], and whether they are removable
questions.question: Let \([\,\cdot\,]\) denote the greatest integer function and \(f(x)=[x]+[-x]\). Which statement describes f correctly?
options: A) f is continuous everywhere and equals 0 for all x
B) \(f(x)=0\) at integers and \(-1\) elsewhere, so f is discontinuous at every integer, and each discontinuity is removable (the limit exists and equals \(-1\))
C) f is discontinuous at every real number
D) \(f(x)=-1\) at integers and 0 elsewhere, with jump discontinuities
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(f=0\) at integers, \(-1\) otherwise; removable discontinuities at every integer.
Given: \(f(x)=[x]+[-x]\)
Formula/Principle: \(x\in\mathbb Z\Rightarrow[x]+[-x]=x-x=0;\ x\notin\mathbb Z\Rightarrow[-x]=-[x]-1\)
Step 1: \(x\notin\mathbb Z:\ f(x)=[x]-[x]-1=-1\)
Step 2: \(\text{at an integer }n:\ \lim_{x\to n}f(x)=-1\ (\text{from both sides}),\ f(n)=0\)
Worked derivation: \[\lim_{x\to n}f(x)=-1\ne0=f(n)\Rightarrow\text{discontinuous; redefining }f(n)=-1\text{ would remove it}\]
Check: \[x=2.3:\ 2+(-3)=-1\ \checkmark;\quad x=2:\ 2+(-2)=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the jumps of }[x]\text{ and }[-x]\text{ at an integer cancel in the limit but not in the value}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f=-1\text{ at non-integers}\); (C) \(f\text{ is constant on each open interval }(n,n+1)\); (D) \(\text{values swapped, and the one-sided limits are equal (no jump)}\).
Key point: \([x]+[-x]=0\text{ at integers},\ -1\text{ otherwise}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Absolute maximum and minimum of a cubic on a closed interval, comparing critical points with end points
questions.question: What are the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of \(f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+5\) on \([-2,6]\)?
options: A) Maximum 10 at \(x=-1\); minimum \(-22\) at \(x=3\)
B) Maximum 10 at \(x=-1\); minimum 3 at \(x=-2\)
C) Maximum 59 at \(x=6\); minimum 3 at \(x=-2\)
D) Maximum 59 at \(x=6\); minimum \(-22\) at \(x=3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Maximum 59 at \(x=6\); minimum \(-22\) at \(x=3\).
Given: \(f'(x)=3x^2-6x-9=3(x-3)(x+1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{compare f at critical points inside the interval and at the end points}\)
Step 1: \(\text{critical points: }x=-1,\ 3\ (\text{both in }[-2,6])\)
Step 2: \(f(-2)=-8-12+18+5=3;\ f(-1)=-1-3+9+5=10\)
Worked derivation: \[f(3)=27-27-27+5=-22;\qquad f(6)=216-108-54+5=59\]
Check: \[\max\{3,10,-22,59\}=59,\ \min=-22\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the local maximum at }x=-1\text{ is not the absolute maximum, because f grows beyond it towards the right end point}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the end point }x=6\); (B) \(\text{ignores }x=3\text{ and }x=6\); (C) \(\text{misses the interior minimum at }x=3\).
Key point: \(\text{absolute extrema on }[a,b]\text{: check critical points and end points}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Definite integrals of the greatest integer function and of |x − 1| read from their graphs
questions.question: What are \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2.5}[x]\,dx\) and \(\displaystyle\int_0^2|x-1|\,dx\), where \([x]\) is the greatest integer function?
options: A) 2 and 1
B) 3 and 1
C) 2 and 0
D) 1.5 and 2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2 and 1.
Given: \([x]=0\text{ on }[0,1),\ 1\text{ on }[1,2),\ 2\text{ on }[2,2.5]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{split the integral where the integrand changes form; read areas of rectangles and triangles}\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2.5}[x]\,dx=0(1)+1(1)+2(0.5)=2\)
Step 2: \(|x-1|\text{ on }[0,2]\text{ forms two triangles, each with base 1 and height 1}\)
Worked derivation: \[\int_0^2|x-1|\,dx=2\times\tfrac12\times1\times1=1\]
Check: \[\int_0^1(1-x)dx+\int_1^2(x-1)dx=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the step graph of }[x]\text{ gives rectangles of width 1 (the last one of width 0.5)}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{takes the last step over a full unit width}\); (C) \(\text{integrates }x-1\text{ without the modulus, so the areas cancel}\); (D) \(\text{misreads both graphs}\).
Key point: \(\text{split at the break points; use areas under the graph}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Area of the smaller segment of a circle cut off by a vertical chord, by integration or the sector formula
questions.question: What is the area of the smaller region cut off from the disc \(x^2+y^2\le16\) by the line \(x=2\)?
options: A) \(\tfrac{16\pi}3+4\sqrt3\)
B) \(\tfrac{8\pi}3-2\sqrt3\)
C) \(\tfrac{16\pi}3-4\sqrt3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\tfrac{16\pi}3-4\sqrt3\).
Given: \(r=4;\ \text{chord }x=2\text{ meets the circle at }(2,\pm2\sqrt3)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{area}=2\displaystyle\int_2^4\sqrt{16-x^2}\,dx;\ \text{or segment}=\tfrac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)\)
Step 1: \(\cos\tfrac\theta2=\tfrac24\Rightarrow\tfrac\theta2=\tfrac\pi3\Rightarrow\theta=\tfrac{2\pi}3\)
Step 2: \(\text{segment}=\tfrac12(16)\left(\tfrac{2\pi}3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{area}=\frac{16\pi}3-4\sqrt3\approx16.76-6.93=9.83\]
Check: \[2\left[\tfrac x2\sqrt{16-x^2}+8\sin^{-1}\tfrac x4\right]_2^4=2\left[4\pi-\left(2\sqrt3+\tfrac{4\pi}3\right)\right]=\tfrac{16\pi}3-4\sqrt3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the segment is the sector of angle }\theta\text{ minus the isosceles triangle formed by the chord and the centre}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{adds the triangle instead of subtracting it}\); (B) \(\text{gives half the segment (one side of the x-axis)}\); (D) \(\text{uses a sector of angle }\tfrac\pi2\).
Key point: \(\text{segment}=\tfrac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving a homogeneous equation by y = vx and finding where the particular solution through a given point exists
questions.question: Solve \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{2xy}\) for the curve through \((2,1)\). For which x (with \(x>0,\ y>0\)) does this solution exist as a real curve?
options: A) \(x^2-y^2=\tfrac32x\); it exists for \(x>\tfrac32\)
B) \(x^2+y^2=\tfrac52x\); it exists for \(0<x<\tfrac52\)
C) \(x^2-y^2=3\); it exists for \(x>\sqrt3\)
D) \(y=\tfrac x2\); it exists for all \(x>0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(x^2-y^2=\tfrac32x\), for \(x>\tfrac32\).
Given: \(\text{homogeneous of degree 0: put }y=vx,\ \dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1+v^2}{2v}\Rightarrow x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1-v^2}{2v}\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{2v\,dv}{1-v^2}=\int\frac{dx}{x}\Rightarrow-\ln|1-v^2|=\ln|x|+c\)
Step 2: \(x(1-v^2)=C\Rightarrow x^2-y^2=Cx;\ (2,1):\ 3=2C\Rightarrow C=\tfrac32\)
Worked derivation: \[y=\sqrt{x^2-\tfrac32x}\ \text{is real and positive for }x>\tfrac32\ (x>0)\]
Check: \[\text{differentiate }x^2-y^2=\tfrac32x:\ 2x-2yy'=\tfrac32,\ y'=\frac{2x-\frac32}{2y};\ \text{using }\tfrac32=\tfrac{x^2-y^2}{x}:\ y'=\frac{x^2+y^2}{2xy}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the solution curve is a hyperbola; its branch through }(2,1)\text{ reaches the x-axis at }x=\tfrac32\text{, where }y=0\text{ and the equation breaks down}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{sign error in the integration}\); (C) \(\text{omits the factor x in }Cx\); (D) \(y=x/2\text{ does not satisfy the equation}\).
Key point: \(\text{homogeneous: }y=vx\text{ separates the variables}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Condition on a for the solution interval of a quadratic inequality to lie inside an open interval of fixed length
questions.question: Let \(A=\{x\in\mathbb R:\ x^2-5x+6\le0\}\) and \(B=(a,\ a+2)\). For which real values of a is \(A\subseteq B\)?
options: A) \(1\le a\le2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(1<a<2\).
Given: \(x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)\le0\iff2\le x\le3\Rightarrow A=[2,3]\)
Formula/Principle: \([p,q]\subseteq(a,b)\iff a<p\text{ and }q<b\)
Step 1: \(a<2\ (\text{so that }2\in B)\)
Step 2: \(a+2>3\iff a>1\ (\text{so that }3\in B)\)
Worked derivation: \[1<a<2\]
Check: \[a=1.5:\ B=(1.5,3.5)\supset[2,3]\ \checkmark;\quad a=1:\ B=(1,3)\not\ni3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a closed interval fits inside an open one only if both its end points lie strictly inside}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{at }a=1\text{ or }a=2\text{ an end point of A falls on an open end of B}\); (B) \(\text{ignores the right end: }a=0\text{ gives }(0,2)\not\supseteq A\); (D) \(\text{then }2\notin B\).
Key point: \([p,q]\subseteq(a,b)\iff a<p,\ q<b;\ \text{open ends exclude equality}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Checking reflexive, symmetric and transitive properties for three relations on the integers
questions.question: On the set of integers, define \(R_1:\ a\,R_1\,b\iff4\mid(a-b)\); \(R_2:\ a\,R_2\,b\iff a\le b\); \(R_3:\ a\,R_3\,b\iff|a-b|\le1\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) All three are equivalence relations
B) \(R_2\) is an equivalence relation and \(R_1\) is not
C) \(R_3\) is transitive but not symmetric
D) \(R_1\) is an equivalence relation with exactly 4 equivalence classes; \(R_2\) is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric; \(R_3\) is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(R_1\): equivalence, 4 classes; \(R_2\): reflexive, transitive, not symmetric; \(R_3\): reflexive, symmetric, not transitive.
Given: \(\text{three relations on }\mathbb Z\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{reflexive: }aRa;\ \text{symmetric: }aRb\Rightarrow bRa;\ \text{transitive: }aRb,\ bRc\Rightarrow aRc\)
Step 1: \(R_1:\ 4\mid0;\ 4\mid(a-b)\Rightarrow4\mid(b-a);\ 4\mid(a-b),\ 4\mid(b-c)\Rightarrow4\mid(a-c)\Rightarrow\text{equivalence; classes are the remainders }0,1,2,3\)
Step 2: \(R_2:\ a\le a;\ a\le b,\ b\le c\Rightarrow a\le c;\ \text{but }1\le2,\ 2\not\le1\)
Worked derivation: \[R_3:\ |0-1|\le1,\ |1-2|\le1,\ \text{but }|0-2|=2>1\Rightarrow\text{not transitive}\]
Check: \[R_3\text{ is reflexive }(|a-a|=0)\text{ and symmetric }(|a-b|=|b-a|)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each property must hold for all elements; one counterexample is enough to fail it}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(R_2\text{ and }R_3\text{ each fail one property}\); (B) \(R_2\text{ is not symmetric, while }R_1\text{ is an equivalence relation}\); (C) \(R_3\text{ is symmetric but not transitive}\).
Key point: \(\text{congruence mod n is an equivalence relation with n classes}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using sum-to-product and product-to-sum formulas to evaluate sin 10° + sin 50° − sin 70° and cos 20° cos 40° cos 80°
questions.question: What are the values of \(\sin10^\circ+\sin50^\circ-\sin70^\circ\) and \(\cos20^\circ\cos40^\circ\cos80^\circ\)?
options: A) \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac18\)
B) \(0\) and \(\tfrac18\)
C) \(0\) and \(\tfrac14\)
D) \(\sin10^\circ\) and \(-\tfrac18\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0 and \(\tfrac18\).
Given: \(\sin C+\sin D=2\sin\tfrac{C+D}2\cos\tfrac{C-D}2;\ 2\cos A\cos B=\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{combine pairs, then use }\sin(90^\circ-\theta)=\cos\theta\)
Step 1: \(\sin50^\circ+\sin10^\circ=2\sin30^\circ\cos20^\circ=\cos20^\circ=\sin70^\circ\Rightarrow\text{sum}=0\)
Step 2: \(\text{multiply the product by }8\sin20^\circ:\ 8\sin20^\circ\cos20^\circ\cos40^\circ\cos80^\circ=4\sin40^\circ\cos40^\circ\cos80^\circ=2\sin80^\circ\cos80^\circ=\sin160^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[\sin160^\circ=\sin20^\circ\Rightarrow\cos20^\circ\cos40^\circ\cos80^\circ=\frac{\sin20^\circ}{8\sin20^\circ}=\frac18\]
Check: \[0.9397\times0.7660\times0.1736=0.1250\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the angles double each time, so repeated use of }2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta\text{ telescopes the product}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes }\sin30^\circ\text{ without the factor 2}\); (C) \(\text{stops one doubling early}\); (D) \(\text{all three cosines are positive, so the product cannot be negative}\).
Key point: \(\sin C+\sin D\text{ formula; }\cos\theta\cos2\theta\cos4\theta=\dfrac{\sin8\theta}{8\sin\theta}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting integer values of k for which x² − kx + 9 = 0 has real roots and for which the roots are equal
questions.question: For how many integers k with \(-10\le k\le10\) does \(x^2-kx+9=0\) have real roots, and for how many of these are the roots equal?
options: A) 21 and 0
B) 12 and 2
C) 10 and 2
D) 10 and 1
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10 and 2.
Given: \(\text{discriminant }D=k^2-36\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{real roots}\iff D\ge0;\ \text{equal roots}\iff D=0\)
Step 1: \(k^2\ge36\iff|k|\ge6\)
Step 2: \(k\in\{-10,\dots,-6\}\cup\{6,\dots,10\}\Rightarrow5+5=10\text{ values}\)
Worked derivation: \[D=0\iff k=\pm6\Rightarrow2\text{ values (roots }x=\pm3)\]
Check: \[k=6:\ x^2-6x+9=(x-3)^2\ \checkmark;\quad k=5:\ D=-11<0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the product of the roots is fixed at 9, so real roots need }|k|=|\text{sum}|\ge2\sqrt9=6\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{counts every integer in the range}\); (B) \(\text{includes }|k|=5\); (D) \(\text{counts only }k=6\text{, missing }k=-6\).
Key point: \(D=b^2-4ac\ge0\text{ for real roots, }=0\text{ for equal roots}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Number of real roots of (x(x − 2))² = k for different k, read from the graph of the left side
questions.question: How many distinct real roots does \(x^4-4x^3+4x^2=k\) have when \(k=\tfrac12\), when \(k=1\), and when \(k=4\)?
options: A) 4, 3 and 2
B) 4, 4 and 2
C) 2, 3 and 4
D) 4, 2 and 0
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4, 3 and 2.
Given: \(x^4-4x^3+4x^2=\left(x(x-2)\right)^2=g(x)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{roots of }g(x)=k\text{ are the intersections of the graph of g with the line }y=k\)
Step 1: \(g\ge0;\ g=0\text{ at }x=0,2\ (\text{minima});\ \text{local maximum }g(1)=1\)
Step 2: \(0<k<1:\ \text{the line cuts each of the two valleys twice: 4 roots};\ k=1:\ \text{touches at the peak }x=1\text{ plus 2 outer roots: 3}\)
Worked derivation: \[k=4:\ x(x-2)=\pm2;\ x^2-2x-2=0\Rightarrow x=1\pm\sqrt3;\ x^2-2x+2=0\text{ has no real roots}\Rightarrow2\]
Check: \[k=1:\ x^2-2x\mp1=0\Rightarrow x=1\pm\sqrt2\text{ or }x=1\ (\text{double})\Rightarrow3\text{ distinct}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the graph is W-shaped with a hump of height 1 at }x=1\text{, so the count changes at }k=0\text{ and }k=1\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{counts the double root at }x=1\text{ twice}\); (C) \(\text{reverses the pattern}\); (D) \(\text{misses the outer roots for }k\ge1\).
Key point: \(\text{count roots of }g(x)=k\text{ from the graph of g}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the number of objects from the count of arrangements with two particular objects together, then the count with them apart
questions.question: When n distinct books are arranged in a row, the number of arrangements in which two particular books are always together is 240. What is n, and in how many arrangements are these two books never together?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(n=6;\ 480\).
Given: \(\text{together}=240\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{treat the pair as one unit: }(n-1)!\text{ arrangements of units}\times2!\text{ inside the pair}\)
Step 1: \(2(n-1)!=240\Rightarrow(n-1)!=120=5!\Rightarrow n=6\)
Step 2: \(\text{total}=6!=720\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{never together}=720-240=480\]
Check: \[\text{gap method: arrange 4 others in }4!=24\text{ ways, choose 2 of 5 gaps in order: }5\times4=20;\ 24\times20=480\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{"never together" is the complement of "always together" within all arrangements}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2\cdot4!=48\ne240\); (B) \(2\cdot6!=1440\ne240\); (C) \(\text{gives the "together" count again}\).
Key point: \(\text{together: }2!(n-1)!;\ \text{apart}=n!-2!(n-1)!\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding n from three consecutive binomial coefficients in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3, and the middle term
questions.question: Three consecutive coefficients in the expansion of \((1+x)^n\) are in the ratio \(1:2:3\). What is n, and what is the coefficient of the middle term of \((1+x)^n\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(n=14;\ 3432\).
Given: \(\binom n{r-1}:\binom nr:\binom n{r+1}=1:2:3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{\binom nr}{\binom n{r-1}}=\dfrac{n-r+1}{r}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{n-r+1}{r}=2\Rightarrow n=3r-1\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{\binom n{r+1}}{\binom nr}=\dfrac{n-r}{r+1}=\dfrac32\Rightarrow2n-2r=3r+3\Rightarrow2n=5r+3\)
Worked derivation: \[2(3r-1)=5r+3\Rightarrow r=5,\ n=14;\quad \text{middle term }T_8:\ \binom{14}7=3432\]
Check: \[\binom{14}4=1001,\ \binom{14}5=2002,\ \binom{14}6=3003:\ 1:2:3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{ratios of consecutive binomial coefficients are simple fractions, giving two linear equations in n and r}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(n=12\text{ has no three consecutive coefficients in this ratio}\); (C) \(3003=\binom{14}6\text{ is one of the three coefficients, not the middle term}\); (D) \(n=15\text{ has two middle terms}\).
Key point: \(\binom nr/\binom n{r-1}=(n-r+1)/r;\ \text{middle term of }(1+x)^{2m}\text{ is }T_{m+1}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the temperature of a copper coil from the rise in its resistance, and contrasting a semiconductor thermistor
questions.question: A copper coil has a resistance of 10.0 Ω at 20 °C. When a current flows for some time, its resistance is measured as 12.0 Ω. The temperature coefficient of resistance of copper is 4.0 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹. What is the coil's temperature, and how would a semiconductor thermistor behave if heated in the same way?
options: A) 50 °C; the thermistor's resistance also rises
B) 520 °C; the thermistor's resistance falls
C) 70 °C; the thermistor's resistance stays the same
D) 70 °C; the thermistor's resistance falls, because more charge carriers are freed as the temperature rises
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 70 °C; the thermistor's resistance falls.
Given: \(R_0=10.0\ \Omega\text{ at }20^\circ\mathrm C,\ R=12.0\ \Omega,\ \alpha=4.0\times10^{-3}\ ^\circ\mathrm C^{-1}\)
Formula/Principle: \(R=R_0\left[1+\alpha(T-T_0)\right]\ (\text{for small temperature ranges})\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{R}{R_0}=1.2=1+4.0\times10^{-3}\,\Delta T\)
Step 2: \(\Delta T=\dfrac{0.2}{4.0\times10^{-3}}=50\ ^\circ\mathrm C\)
Worked derivation: \[T=20+50=70\ ^\circ\mathrm C\]
Check: \[10.0\left[1+0.004\times50\right]=12.0\ \Omega\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in a metal, the number of free electrons is fixed, but hotter ions vibrate more and scatter electrons more often, so resistivity rises; in a semiconductor, heating frees many more carriers, which outweighs the extra scattering}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{gives the rise in temperature, not the final temperature, and gets the thermistor wrong}\); (B) \(\text{uses }\alpha\text{ as }4\times10^{-4}\); (C) \(\text{a thermistor's resistance depends strongly on temperature}\).
Key point: \(\text{metals: }R=R_0(1+\alpha\Delta T),\ \alpha>0;\ \text{semiconductors: R falls with T}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Radius and period of a proton's circular path in a magnetic field after acceleration through 1.0 kV, using energy conservation
questions.question: A proton, initially at rest, is accelerated through a potential difference of 1.0 kV and then enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.10 T at right angles to the field. What is its speed, the radius of its circular path and its period of revolution? What happens to the radius and period if the accelerating voltage is made four times larger? (m_p = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
options: A) 4.4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; 4.6 cm; 0.66 µs; radius ×4, period ×2
B) 1.9 × 10¹¹ m s⁻¹; 4.6 cm; 0.66 µs; radius ×2, period ×2
C) 4.4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; 4.6 cm; 0.66 µs; radius ×2, period unchanged
D) 4.4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; 2.3 cm; 1.3 µs; radius ×2, period ×½
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4.4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹; 4.6 cm; 0.66 µs; radius doubles, period unchanged.
Given: \(V=1.0\times10^3\ \mathrm V,\ B=0.10\ \mathrm T,\ m=1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg},\ q=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{energy: }qV=\tfrac12mv^2;\ \text{circular motion: }qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow r=\dfrac{mv}{qB},\ T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}\)
Step 1: \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2qV}{m}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times10^3}{1.67\times10^{-27}}}=\sqrt{1.92\times10^{11}}=4.38\times10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(r=\dfrac{1.67\times10^{-27}\times4.38\times10^5}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.10}=4.57\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m\)
Worked derivation: \[T=\frac{2\pi\times1.67\times10^{-27}}{1.6\times10^{-20}}=6.56\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm s;\qquad r\propto v\propto\sqrt V\Rightarrow V\times4:\ r\times2\]
Check: \[T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=\frac{2\pi\times0.0457}{4.38\times10^5}=6.56\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm s\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the kinetic energy (speed) stays constant; a faster particle moves on a larger circle in the same time}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes }r\propto V\text{ and makes the period depend on speed}\); (B) \(\text{gives }v^2\text{ as the speed}\); (D) \(\text{halves the radius (uses 2qB) and makes T depend on speed}\).
Key point: \(qV=\tfrac12mv^2;\ r=mv/qB;\ T=2\pi m/qB\text{ is independent of speed}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Work done in pulling a square loop out of a magnetic field at constant speed, equal to the heat produced (Lenz's law and energy conservation)
questions.question: A square wire loop of side 0.10 m and resistance 0.50 Ω lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.40 T that ends sharply at one edge of the field region. The loop is pulled out of the field at a constant 2.0 m s⁻¹, one side always parallel to the field boundary. What is the induced current, the force needed, and the work done in pulling the loop completely out?
options: B) 0.16 A; 6.4 × 10⁻³ N; 6.4 × 10⁻⁴ J, all of it appearing as heat in the loop
D) 0.16 A; zero force, because the loop moves at constant speed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.16 A; 6.4 × 10⁻³ N; 6.4 × 10⁻⁴ J, all converted to heat.
Given: \(l=0.10\ \mathrm m,\ R=0.50\ \Omega,\ B=0.40\ \mathrm T,\ v=2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Faraday: }\varepsilon=Blv;\ I=\varepsilon/R;\ \text{force on the side in the field: }F=BIl;\ W=Fl\)
Step 1: \(\varepsilon=0.40\times0.10\times2.0=0.080\ \mathrm V;\ I=\dfrac{0.080}{0.50}=0.16\ \mathrm A\)
Step 2: \(F=0.40\times0.16\times0.10=6.4\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm N\)
Worked derivation: \[W=F\times l=6.4\times10^{-3}\times0.10=6.4\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[\text{time}=\frac{0.10}{2.0}=0.050\ \mathrm s;\ I^2Rt=0.0256\times0.50\times0.050=6.4\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm J\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{by Lenz's law the induced current opposes the decrease in flux, so the field pulls back on the loop; the work done against this force is exactly the energy dissipated as heat, as conservation of energy requires}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses the loop's full perimeter for the force}\); (C) \(\text{doubles the emf by counting two sides}\); (D) \(\text{constant speed means the applied force balances the magnetic drag; it is not zero}\).
Key point: \(\varepsilon=Blv;\ \text{work against magnetic drag}=I^2Rt\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Peak power, half-power frequencies and sharpness of the average power against frequency curve of a series LCR circuit
questions.question: A series circuit has R = 20 Ω, L = 0.50 H and C = 2.0 µF, driven by a 100 V (rms) source of variable angular frequency ω. Which description of the graph of average power P against ω is correct?
options: A) P peaks at ω₀ = 1000 rad s⁻¹ with P_max = 500 W; P falls to 250 W at about 980 and 1020 rad s⁻¹ (bandwidth 40 rad s⁻¹, quality factor 25); with a smaller R, the peak would be higher and narrower
B) P peaks at ω₀ = 1000 rad s⁻¹ with P_max = 5.0 W
C) P rises steadily with ω and has no peak
D) P peaks at ω₀ = 1000 rad s⁻¹ with P_max = 500 W; a smaller R would give a lower, broader peak
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ω₀ = 1000 rad s⁻¹; P_max = 500 W; half-power points 980 and 1020 rad s⁻¹; smaller R gives a sharper peak.
Given: \(R=20\ \Omega,\ L=0.50\ \mathrm H,\ C=2.0\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm F,\ V=100\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(\omega_0=\dfrac1{\sqrt{LC}};\ P=I^2R=\dfrac{V^2R}{Z^2};\ \text{half-power points: }\omega_0\pm\dfrac{R}{2L};\ Q=\dfrac{\omega_0L}{R}\)
Step 1: \(\omega_0=\dfrac1{\sqrt{0.50\times2.0\times10^{-6}}}=\dfrac1{10^{-3}}=1000\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(P_{\max}=\dfrac{V^2}{R}=\dfrac{10^4}{20}=500\ \mathrm W\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac R{2L}=\frac{20}{1.0}=20\Rightarrow\omega=980,\ 1020\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}};\quad Q=\frac{1000\times0.50}{20}=25=\frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}\]
Check: \[\text{at half power, }|X_L-X_C|=R\Rightarrow Z=\sqrt2R\Rightarrow P=\frac{V^2}{2R}=250\ \mathrm W\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the power is greatest when the reactances cancel; the width of the peak is set by R/L, so lowering R makes it taller }(V^2/R)\text{ and narrower}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses }V/R\text{ squared wrongly (}I^2\text{ without R)}\); (C) \(\text{a series LCR circuit always shows resonance}\); (D) \(\text{reverses the effect of R}\).
Key point: \(P_{\max}=V^2/R\text{ at }\omega_0;\ \Delta\omega=R/L;\ Q=\omega_0/\Delta\omega\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Power of two thin lenses in contact and separated, and the image formed by the combination in contact
questions.question: A thin lens of power +5.0 D is placed in contact with a thin lens of power −2.0 D. An object is placed 50 cm in front of the combination. Where is the image, and what is the magnification? What would the power of the combination be if the lenses were separated by 10 cm?
options: A) Image 25 cm behind; magnification −0.5; power 3.0 D
B) Image 100 cm behind the lens; magnification −2; power 4.0 D when separated by 10 cm
C) Image 33 cm behind; magnification −0.67; power 2.0 D
D) Image 100 cm in front (virtual); magnification +2; power 4.0 D
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Image 100 cm behind; magnification −2; 4.0 D when separated.
Given: \(P_1=+5.0\ \mathrm D,\ P_2=-2.0\ \mathrm D,\ u=-0.50\ \mathrm m,\ d=0.10\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{in contact: }P=P_1+P_2;\ \text{separated: }P=P_1+P_2-dP_1P_2;\ \dfrac1v-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f=P;\ m=\dfrac vu\)
Step 1: \(P=+3.0\ \mathrm D\Rightarrow f=33.3\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac1v=3.0+\dfrac1{-0.50}=3.0-2.0=1.0\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\Rightarrow v=+1.00\ \mathrm m\)
Worked derivation: \[m=\frac{1.00}{-0.50}=-2;\qquad P_{\text{sep}}=3.0-0.10\times5.0\times(-2.0)=4.0\ \mathrm D\]
Check: \[\text{object between f and 2f }(33\text{ cm}<50\text{ cm}<67\text{ cm})\Rightarrow\text{real, inverted, magnified image beyond 2f}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{powers of thin lenses in contact add; separating a converging and a diverging lens changes the total because light reaches the second lens at a different height}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }P=P_1\text{ only for the image}\); (C) \(\text{places the image at the focus, as for a distant object}\); (D) \(\text{sign error: a real image forms because the object is beyond f}\).
Key point: \(P=P_1+P_2\text{ (contact)};\ P=P_1+P_2-dP_1P_2\text{ (separated)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Work function and threshold from a measured stopping potential, and how stopping potential and photocurrent depend on wavelength and intensity
questions.question: In a photoelectric experiment, light of wavelength 400 nm gives a stopping potential of 1.0 V. What is the work function of the metal, what stopping potential would 300 nm light give, and what happens when the intensity of the 400 nm light is doubled? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
options: A) 3.1 eV; 4.1 V; the stopping potential doubles
B) 1.0 eV; 3.1 V; the current is unchanged
C) 2.1 eV; 2.0 V; the stopping potential doubles and the current is unchanged
D) 2.1 eV; about 2.0 V; the saturation current doubles, but the stopping potential stays 1.0 V; the threshold wavelength is about 590 nm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) φ = 2.1 eV; V₀ ≈ 2.0 V at 300 nm; doubling intensity doubles the saturation current only; λ₀ ≈ 590 nm.
Given: \(\lambda_1=400\ \mathrm{nm},\ V_1=1.0\ \mathrm V,\ \lambda_2=300\ \mathrm{nm},\ hc=1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Einstein: }eV_0=\dfrac{hc}\lambda-\phi\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{1240}{400}=3.10\ \mathrm{eV}\Rightarrow\phi=3.10-1.0=2.10\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1240}{300}=4.13\ \mathrm{eV}\Rightarrow V_0=4.13-2.10=2.03\ \mathrm V\)
Worked derivation: \[\lambda_0=\frac{1240}{2.10}\approx590\ \mathrm{nm}\]
Check: \[\text{difference in }V_0=\Delta\left(\frac{hc}{\lambda}\right)/e=4.13-3.10=1.03\ \mathrm V\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each photon frees at most one electron, with energy fixed by its frequency; more intense light means more photons per second and so more electrons, but not faster ones}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes the photon energy as the work function, and intensity does not change }V_0\); (B) \(\text{takes the stopping potential as the work function}\); (C) \(\text{reverses the effect of intensity}\).
Key point: \(eV_0=hc/\lambda-\phi;\ \text{intensity changes the current, not }V_0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Distance of closest approach of an α-particle to a gold nucleus from energy conservation, and the energy needed to reach the nuclear surface
questions.question: An α-particle of kinetic energy 5.0 MeV is fired head-on at a gold nucleus (Z = 79), treated as fixed. What is the distance of closest approach? What kinetic energy would be needed to bring it to 7.0 fm from the centre (roughly the gold nuclear radius), and what happens to the closest approach if the 5.0 MeV energy is doubled? (ke² = 1.44 MeV fm)
options: A) About 45 fm; about 32 MeV; it halves
B) About 23 fm; about 16 MeV; it halves
C) About 45 fm; about 32 MeV; it is reduced by a factor √2
D) About 91 fm; about 65 MeV; it doubles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) About 45 fm; about 32 MeV; it halves.
Given: \(K=5.0\ \mathrm{MeV};\ q_\alpha=2e,\ Q=79e;\ ke^2=1.44\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{energy conservation: at closest approach all KE becomes electric PE: }K=\dfrac{k(2e)(79e)}{d}\)
Step 1: \(k(2)(79)e^2=158\times1.44=227.5\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}\)
Step 2: \(d=\dfrac{227.5}{5.0}=45.5\ \mathrm{fm}\)
Worked derivation: \[K_{7\ \mathrm{fm}}=\frac{227.5}{7.0}=32.5\ \mathrm{MeV};\qquad d\propto\frac1K\Rightarrow K\times2:\ d\to22.8\ \mathrm{fm}\]
Check: \[45.5\ \mathrm{fm}\gg7\ \mathrm{fm}\Rightarrow\text{at 5 MeV the alpha particle never reaches the nucleus, so pure Coulomb scattering applies}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{Rutherford could treat the nucleus as a point charge because his alpha particles stopped far outside it; this distance gave an upper limit on the nuclear size}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses charge e instead of 2e for the alpha particle}\); (C) \(\text{takes d as proportional to }1/\sqrt K\); (D) \(\text{doubles the product of charges, and closest approach decreases as K rises}\).
Key point: \(d=k(2e)(Ze)/K;\ d\propto1/K\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Density of nuclear matter from R = R₀A^(1/3), applied to estimate the radius of a neutron star, and the properties of the nuclear force
questions.question: Using R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ = 1.2 fm and a nucleon mass of 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, estimate the density of nuclear matter. If a star of mass 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg collapsed to this density (a neutron star), what would its radius be? Which statement about the nuclear force is also correct?
options: A) About 2.3 × 10³ kg m⁻³; about 600 km; the nuclear force is long-range like gravity
B) About 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³; about 1300 km; the nuclear force acts only between protons
C) About 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, the same for all nuclei; about 13 km; the nuclear force is very strong, short-range (a few fm), nearly the same between any pair of nucleons, and saturates
D) About 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³; about 13 km; the nuclear force is weaker than the electric force between protons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ρ ≈ 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³; radius ≈ 13 km; strong, short-range, charge-independent, saturating force.
Given: \(R_0=1.2\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm m,\ m=1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg},\ M=2.0\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\rho=\dfrac{Am}{\frac43\pi R_0^3A}=\dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}\ (\text{independent of A});\ R_{\text{star}}=\left(\dfrac{3M}{4\pi\rho}\right)^{1/3}\)
Step 1: \(\rho=\dfrac{3\times1.67\times10^{-27}}{4\pi\times1.728\times10^{-45}}=\dfrac{5.01\times10^{-27}}{2.17\times10^{-44}}\approx2.3\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)
Step 2: \(V=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{30}}{2.3\times10^{17}}=8.7\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{m^3}\)
Worked derivation: \[R=\left(\frac{3\times8.7\times10^{12}}{4\pi}\right)^{1/3}=(2.08\times10^{12})^{1/3}\approx1.3\times10^4\ \mathrm m\]
Check: \[\frac43\pi(1.28\times10^4)^3\times2.3\times10^{17}\approx8.8\times10^{12}\times2.3\times10^{17}\approx2.0\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{nuclear volume is proportional to A, so all nuclei have the same density; this follows from the short range and saturation of the nuclear force, which binds each nucleon only to its near neighbours}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses the factor }10^{-45}\text{ in }R_0^3\text{, and the nuclear force is short-range}\); (B) \(\text{wrong cube root, and the force acts between all nucleons, including neutrons}\); (D) \(\text{the nuclear force is much stronger than the electric repulsion at nuclear distances}\).
Key point: \(\rho_{\text{nuc}}=3m/(4\pi R_0^3)\approx2.3\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\text{ for all A}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Electron and hole concentrations in germanium doped with boron at one part in 10⁷, using the mass action law
questions.question: Pure germanium has 4.4 × 10²⁸ atoms m⁻³ and an intrinsic carrier concentration of 2.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³ at room temperature. It is doped with boron at a level of one boron atom per 10⁷ germanium atoms. What are the hole and electron concentrations, and what type of semiconductor results?
options: A) Holes 2.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³, electrons 2.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³; intrinsic
B) Electrons 4.4 × 10²¹ m⁻³, holes 1.3 × 10¹⁷ m⁻³; n-type
C) Holes 4.4 × 10²¹ m⁻³, electrons about 1.3 × 10¹⁷ m⁻³; p-type
D) Holes 4.4 × 10²¹ m⁻³, electrons 4.4 × 10²¹ m⁻³; p-type
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Holes 4.4 × 10²¹ m⁻³; electrons ≈ 1.3 × 10¹⁷ m⁻³; p-type.
Given: \(N_{\mathrm{Ge}}=4.4\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}},\ n_i=2.4\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}},\ \text{doping }1:10^7\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{trivalent B is an acceptor: }n_h\approx N_A;\ \text{mass action law: }n_en_h=n_i^2\)
Step 1: \(N_A=\dfrac{4.4\times10^{28}}{10^7}=4.4\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\gg n_i\Rightarrow n_h\approx4.4\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\)
Step 2: \(n_e=\dfrac{n_i^2}{n_h}=\dfrac{(2.4\times10^{19})^2}{4.4\times10^{21}}=\dfrac{5.76\times10^{38}}{4.4\times10^{21}}\)
Worked derivation: \[n_e\approx1.3\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\]
Check: \[n_en_h=1.31\times10^{17}\times4.4\times10^{21}=5.76\times10^{38}=n_i^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each boron atom accepts an electron from the lattice, creating a hole; the many extra holes recombine with thermally produced electrons, lowering the electron concentration below }n_i\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the doping}\); (B) \(\text{boron (group 13) creates holes, not free electrons}\); (D) \(\text{electrons and holes are not equal in a doped semiconductor}\).
Key point: \(\text{acceptor doping: }n_h\approx N_A,\ n_e=n_i^2/N_A\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Average and instantaneous velocity, average speed and turning points from the position–time graph x = t³ − 6t² + 9t
questions.question: A particle moves along x with position \(x=t^3-6t^2+9t\) (x in metres, t in seconds). Its x–t graph rises to a peak at t = 1 s, falls to zero at t = 3 s, and rises again. For the interval t = 0 to t = 4 s, what are the average velocity, the instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s, the distance travelled and the average speed?
options: A) 1 m s⁻¹; −3 m s⁻¹; 12 m; 3 m s⁻¹
B) 1 m s⁻¹; +3 m s⁻¹; 4 m; 1 m s⁻¹
C) 0; −3 m s⁻¹; 12 m; 3 m s⁻¹
D) 3 m s⁻¹; 0; 12 m; 1 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1 m s⁻¹; −3 m s⁻¹; 12 m; 3 m s⁻¹.
Given: \(x(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t;\ x(0)=0,\ x(1)=4,\ x(3)=0,\ x(4)=4\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(\bar v=\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t};\ v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}\ (\text{slope of the tangent});\ \text{distance}=\text{sum of }|\Delta x|\text{ between turning points}\)
Step 1: \(\bar v=\dfrac{4-0}{4}=1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(v=3t^2-12t+9=3(t-1)(t-3);\ v(2)=12-24+9=-3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{distance}=|4-0|+|0-4|+|4-0|=12\ \mathrm m;\quad \text{average speed}=\frac{12}{4}=3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[v=0\text{ at }t=1,3\text{ (peak and trough of the graph), where the particle turns}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{average velocity uses only the net displacement, while average speed uses the total path length, which includes the motion back and forth}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the slope at t = 2 s is negative (the graph is falling), and the distance is not the displacement}\); (C) \(\text{the net displacement is 4 m, not 0}\); (D) \(\text{confuses average velocity with average speed and puts the turning point at t = 2 s}\).
Key point: \(\text{average velocity}=\Delta x/\Delta t;\ \text{average speed}=\text{path}/\text{time};\ v=dx/dt\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Position, velocity and path of a puck on an air table with a constant initial velocity and a perpendicular constant acceleration
questions.question: A puck on a level, frictionless air table is moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ along +x when, at t = 0 and at the origin, a steady air jet begins to give it a constant acceleration of 2.0 m s⁻² along +y. A strobe photograph records its positions. Where is the puck at t = 2.0 s, what is its velocity then, and what is the equation of its path?
options: A) \((6.0,\ 2.0)\) m; 3.6 m s⁻¹ at 34° to the x-axis; a straight line \(y=x/3\)
D) \((6.0,\ 4.0)\) m; 5.0 m s⁻¹ at about 53° to the x-axis; a parabola \(y=x^2/9\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \((6.0,4.0)\) m; 5.0 m s⁻¹ at 53°; \(y=x^2/9\).
Given: \(\vec u=(3.0,\,0)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ \vec a=(0,\,2.0)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\ t=2.0\ \mathrm s\)
Formula/Principle: \(\vec r=\vec ut+\tfrac12\vec at^2;\ \vec v=\vec u+\vec at\ (\text{each component separately})\)
Step 1: \(x=3.0\times2.0=6.0\ \mathrm m;\ y=\tfrac12\times2.0\times4.0=4.0\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(v_x=3.0,\ v_y=2.0\times2.0=4.0\Rightarrow v=5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ \tan\theta=\tfrac43\Rightarrow\theta\approx53^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[x=3t,\ y=t^2\Rightarrow y=\frac{x^2}{9}\]
Check: \[x=6.0:\ y=\frac{36}{9}=4.0\ \mathrm m\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{motion in a plane with constant acceleration splits into independent motions along x (uniform) and y (uniformly accelerated), giving a parabolic path, as for a projectile}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{omits the factor t in }v_y\text{ and treats y as uniform}\); (B) \(\text{adds the speed components arithmetically}\); (C) \(\text{takes x as }3.0\ \mathrm m\text{ and ignores }v_x\).
Key point: \(\text{constant }\vec a:\ \vec r=\vec ut+\tfrac12\vec at^2;\ \perp\vec u\text{ gives a parabola}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Minimum speeds and the tension difference between the bottom and top of a vertical circle, for a string and for a rigid rod
questions.question: A small mass m moves in a vertical circle of radius R. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The minimum speed at the top is zero for a string, because tension can be negative

B) For a string, the minimum speed at the top is \(\sqrt{gR}\) and at the bottom \(\sqrt{5gR}\); whenever the mass completes the circle, the tension at the bottom exceeds that at the top by 6mg, whatever the speed; for a mass on a light rigid rod, the speed at the top can be almost zero, so the minimum speed at the bottom is \(\sqrt{4gR}\)
C) The tension is the same at the top and bottom, because the speed is constant
D) The minimum speed at the bottom is \(\sqrt{2gR}\) for both a string and a rod
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) String: \(\sqrt{gR}\) at top, \(\sqrt{5gR}\) at bottom, \(T_b-T_t=6mg\); rod: \(\sqrt{4gR}\) at bottom.
Given: \(\text{radius }R;\ \text{only gravity and tension (or rod force) act; no friction}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{top: }T_t+mg=\dfrac{mv_t^2}{R};\ \text{bottom: }T_b-mg=\dfrac{mv_b^2}{R};\ \text{energy: }v_b^2=v_t^2+4gR\)
Step 1: \(\text{string: }T_t\ge0\Rightarrow v_t^2\ge gR\Rightarrow v_b^2\ge5gR\)
Step 2: \(T_b-T_t=\dfrac{m(v_b^2-v_t^2)}{R}+2mg=4mg+2mg=6mg\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{rod: it can push as well as pull, so }v_t\to0\text{ is allowed}\Rightarrow v_b^2\ge4gR\]
Check: \[v_t^2=gR:\ T_t=0,\ T_b=6mg\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a string can only pull, so at the top gravity alone must be able to provide the centripetal force; a rod can support the mass from below}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{a string cannot push, so tension cannot be negative}\); (C) \(\text{the speed is not constant in a vertical circle; gravity speeds the mass up on the way down}\); (D) \(\sqrt{2gR}\text{ only lets the mass rise to the level of the centre}\).
Key point: \(\text{string: }v_t\ge\sqrt{gR},\ v_b\ge\sqrt{5gR},\ T_b-T_t=6mg;\ \text{rod: }v_b\ge\sqrt{4gR}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Shape of the gravitational potential energy curve outside the Earth and the escape speed derived from it
questions.question: Which statement about the graph of gravitational potential energy U of a body of mass m against distance r from the centre of the Earth (r ≥ R), and the escape speed, is correct? (g = 9.8 m s⁻², R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m)
options: A) U is positive and decreases as r increases
B) U is zero at the surface and increases linearly with r for all distances
C) The escape speed depends on the mass of the body and on the direction in which it is thrown

D) U = −GMm/r is negative, rising towards zero as r → ∞ (a curve that is steep near the surface and flattens out); a body escapes if its kinetic energy can make its total energy zero, giving \(v_e=\sqrt{2GM/R}=\sqrt{2gR}\approx11.2\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), independent of its mass and of the direction of launch (ignoring air)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) U negative, rising to zero; \(v_e=\sqrt{2gR}\approx11.2\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\).
Given: \(U(r)=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}\ (U=0\text{ at infinity});\ g=\dfrac{GM}{R^2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{escape: }\tfrac12mv_e^2-\dfrac{GMm}{R}=0\)
Step 1: \(v_e=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}=\sqrt{2gR}\)
Step 2: \(v_e=\sqrt{2\times9.8\times6.4\times10^6}=\sqrt{1.25\times10^8}\)
Worked derivation: \[v_e\approx1.12\times10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}=11.2\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[\text{near the surface, }\Delta U\approx mgh\text{ (the curve looks linear over small heights)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{energy is a scalar, so the direction of launch does not matter; both KE and PE are proportional to m, so m cancels}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{with }U=0\text{ at infinity, U is negative and increases with r}\); (B) \(mgh\text{ is only a near-surface approximation}\); (C) \(m\text{ cancels, and direction does not enter an energy balance}\).
Key point: \(U=-GMm/r;\ v_e=\sqrt{2gR}\approx11.2\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the viscosity of glycerine from the terminal speed of a falling steel ball using Stokes' law
questions.question: A steel ball of radius 1.0 mm (density 7800 kg m⁻³) is dropped into a tall jar of glycerine (density 1260 kg m⁻³). After a short distance it falls at a steady 1.0 cm s⁻¹. What is the viscosity of glycerine, and what is the net force on the ball while it falls at this steady speed? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
options: A) 0.15 Pa s; equal to its weight
B) About 1.5 Pa s; zero, because weight is balanced by buoyancy plus viscous drag
C) About 1.5 Pa s; equal to the buoyant force
D) 14.5 Pa s; zero
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) About 1.5 Pa s; the net force is zero.
Given: \(r=1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m,\ \rho=7800,\ \sigma=1260\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}},\ v_t=1.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{at terminal speed: }\tfrac43\pi r^3\rho g=\tfrac43\pi r^3\sigma g+6\pi\eta rv_t\Rightarrow\eta=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9v_t}\)
Step 1: \(2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g=2\times10^{-6}\times6540\times10=0.1308\)
Step 2: \(9v_t=9\times10^{-2}=0.09\)
Worked derivation: \[\eta=\frac{0.1308}{0.09}\approx1.45\ \mathrm{Pa\,s}\]
Check: \[\text{drag}=6\pi\eta rv_t=6\pi\times1.45\times10^{-3}\times10^{-2}=2.74\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm N;\ \text{weight}-\text{buoyancy}=\tfrac43\pi(10^{-9})(6540)(10)=2.74\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm N\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the drag grows with speed until the forces balance; after that the ball moves with constant velocity (zero acceleration)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{a factor of 10 error, and at terminal speed the net force is zero}\); (C) \(\text{there is no net force at terminal speed}\); (D) \(\text{uses }v_t=1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
Key point: \(\eta=2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g/(9v_t);\ \text{net force zero at terminal speed}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Junction temperature and heat current for two rods of different conductivity joined in series, compared with the same rods in parallel
questions.question: Two rods of the same length and cross-section have thermal conductivities k₁ = 2k and k₂ = k. (i) They are joined end to end, with the free end of rod 1 at 100 °C and that of rod 2 at 0 °C. (ii) They are placed side by side between the same two reservoirs. What is the junction temperature in (i), and what is the ratio of the total heat current in (ii) to that in (i)? (No heat is lost from the sides.)
options: A) About 66.7 °C; 4.5
C) About 33.3 °C; 4.5
D) About 66.7 °C; 2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) About 66.7 °C; 4.5.
Given: \(k_1=2k,\ k_2=k;\ \text{same }L,\ A;\ T_H=100^\circ\mathrm C,\ T_C=0^\circ\mathrm C\)
Formula/Principle: \(H=\dfrac{kA\Delta T}{L};\ \text{in series, the same H flows through both rods}\)
Step 1: \(2k(100-T)=k(T-0)\Rightarrow200=3T\Rightarrow T=66.7^\circ\mathrm C\)
Step 2: \(H_s=\dfrac{kA}{L}(66.7)=\dfrac23\cdot\dfrac{kA\times100}{L}\)
Worked derivation: \[H_p=(2k+k)\frac{A\times100}{L}=3\cdot\frac{kA\times100}{L};\qquad \frac{H_p}{H_s}=\frac{3}{2/3}=4.5\]
Check: \[\text{series thermal resistances: }\frac{L}{2kA}+\frac{L}{kA}=\frac{3L}{2kA}\Rightarrow H_s=\frac{2kA\times100}{3L}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the better conductor needs a smaller temperature drop to carry the same heat, so the junction is closer to the hot end}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{assumes equal conductivities}\); (C) \(\text{puts the larger temperature drop across the better conductor}\); (D) \(\text{the junction is right, but series and parallel resistances combine differently, giving 4.5}\).
Key point: \(\text{series: same H, add }L/kA;\ \text{parallel: add }kA/L\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Heat, work and internal energy change when 2 mol of a monatomic gas is heated by 50 K at constant volume and at constant pressure
questions.question: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas are heated by 50 K, once at constant volume and once at constant pressure. What are the heat supplied, the work done by the gas and the change in internal energy in each case? (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
options: A) Constant V: 1247 J, 0, 1247 J; constant P: 2078 J, 831 J, 2078 J
B) Constant V: 2078 J, 831 J, 1247 J; constant P: 1247 J, 0, 1247 J
C) Constant V: Q = 1247 J, W = 0, ΔU = 1247 J; constant P: Q = 2078 J, W = 831 J, ΔU = 1247 J
D) Both cases: Q = 1247 J, W = 0, ΔU = 1247 J
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) V constant: 1247 J, 0, 1247 J; P constant: 2078 J, 831 J, 1247 J.
Given: \(n=2,\ \Delta T=50\ \mathrm K;\ C_v=\tfrac32R,\ C_p=\tfrac52R\ (\text{monatomic})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta U=nC_v\Delta T\ (\text{any process});\ Q=\Delta U+W;\ W=P\Delta V=nR\Delta T\text{ at constant P}\)
Step 1: \(\Delta U=2\times\tfrac32\times8.31\times50=1247\ \mathrm J\ (\text{same in both cases})\)
Step 2: \(\text{constant V: }W=0,\ Q=1247\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{constant P: }W=2\times8.31\times50=831\ \mathrm J;\quad Q=nC_p\Delta T=2\times\tfrac52\times8.31\times50=2078\ \mathrm J=1247+831\]
Check: \[Q_p-Q_v=nR\Delta T=831\ \mathrm J\ (\text{this is why }C_p-C_v=R)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, so it changes equally; at constant pressure extra heat is needed for the work of expansion}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\Delta U\text{ is the same for the same temperature change}\); (B) \(\text{swaps the two cases}\); (D) \(\text{at constant pressure the gas expands and does work}\).
Key point: \(\Delta U=nC_v\Delta T\text{ always};\ Q_p=Q_v+nR\Delta T\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Amplitude, period, initial displacement and velocity, maximum acceleration and first time at the extreme for x = 0.05 sin(10πt + π/6)
questions.question: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion according to \(x=0.05\sin\left(10\pi t+\dfrac\pi6\right)\), with x in metres and t in seconds. What are its period, its displacement and velocity at t = 0, its maximum acceleration, and the first time after t = 0 at which it is at x = +0.05 m?
options: A) 0.20 s; 0.025 m and about 1.36 m s⁻¹; about 49 m s⁻²; \(\tfrac1{30}\) s
B) 0.10 s; 0.043 m and 0.79 m s⁻¹; about 49 m s⁻²; \(\tfrac1{20}\) s
C) 0.20 s; 0.025 m and 1.57 m s⁻¹; about 4.9 m s⁻²; \(\tfrac1{20}\) s
D) 5.0 s; 0.025 m and about 1.36 m s⁻¹; about 49 m s⁻²; \(\tfrac1{60}\) s
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.20 s; 0.025 m and 1.36 m s⁻¹; 49 m s⁻²; 1/30 s.
Given: \(A=0.05\ \mathrm m,\ \omega=10\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\ \phi=\tfrac\pi6\)
Formula/Principle: \(T=\dfrac{2\pi}\omega;\ v=A\omega\cos(\omega t+\phi);\ a_{\max}=A\omega^2\)
Step 1: \(T=\dfrac{2\pi}{10\pi}=0.20\ \mathrm s;\ x(0)=0.05\sin\tfrac\pi6=0.025\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(v(0)=0.05\times10\pi\times\cos\tfrac\pi6=1.571\times0.866=1.36\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Worked derivation: \[a_{\max}=0.05\times(10\pi)^2=49.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}};\qquad 10\pi t+\tfrac\pi6=\tfrac\pi2\Rightarrow t=\frac{\pi/3}{10\pi}=\frac1{30}\ \mathrm s\]
Check: \[v^2=\omega^2(A^2-x^2)=(10\pi)^2(0.0025-0.000625)\Rightarrow v=31.42\times0.0433=1.36\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the initial phase }\pi/6\text{ means the particle starts part of the way towards the positive extreme, moving outward, so it reaches }+A\text{ after a phase change of }\pi/3\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses }T=\pi/\omega\text{ and the cosine for the displacement}\); (C) \(\text{ignores the phase in }v(0)\text{ and misplaces a factor of 10 in }a_{\max}\); (D) \(\text{gives the frequency (5 Hz) as the period}\).
Key point: \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi):\ v=A\omega\cos(\cdot),\ a_{\max}=A\omega^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Reflection of a pulse at fixed and free ends and at a junction of strings, and superposition of crossing pulses
questions.question: Which statement about pulses on strings is correct?
options: A) A pulse reflected from a fixed end returns upright, and from a free end it returns inverted
B) When two pulses meet, they bounce off each other and reverse direction
C) A pulse going from a heavy string into a light string is reflected inverted

D) A pulse reflected from a rigidly fixed end returns inverted (a phase change of π), while one reflected from a free end returns upright; at a junction where a light string joins a heavier one, the reflected pulse is inverted and the transmitted pulse is upright; two pulses that meet add their displacements while overlapping and then continue unchanged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Fixed end: inverted; free end: upright; light-to-heavy junction: reflected inverted, transmitted upright; pulses pass through each other.
Given: \(\text{incident pulse }y_i=f(x-vt);\ \text{superposition: }y=y_1+y_2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{fixed end: }y=0\text{ there at all times}\Rightarrow y_r=-f(-x-vt);\ \text{free end: slope zero}\Rightarrow y_r=+f(-x-vt)\)
Step 1: \(\text{at a fixed end the support pulls the string the opposite way, so the reflected pulse is inverted (phase change }\pi)\)
Step 2: \(\text{at a free end the string overshoots and the pulse returns upright (no phase change)}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{junction: }r=\frac{v_2-v_1}{v_1+v_2},\ t=\frac{2v_2}{v_1+v_2};\ \text{light}\to\text{heavy: }v_2<v_1\Rightarrow r<0\ (\text{inverted}),\ t>0\ (\text{upright})\]
Check: \[v_2\to0\ (\text{infinitely heavy, i.e. fixed end}):\ r\to-1\ (\text{inverted, full amplitude})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{waves on a string obey the principle of superposition, so overlapping pulses simply add and then separate unchanged}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{reverses the two cases}\); (B) \(\text{pulses pass through each other}\); (C) \(\text{from a heavy string to a light one, the reflected pulse is upright}\).
Key point: \(\text{fixed end or denser medium: reflected inverted; free end or rarer medium: upright}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Electric flux through the faces of a cube with a charge at its centre, displaced inside it, or outside it
questions.question: A point charge q is placed at the centre of an imaginary cube. Which statement about the electric flux through the cube is correct?
options: A) The flux through each face is \(q/\varepsilon_0\)

B) The flux through each face is \(q/6\varepsilon_0\); if the charge is moved off-centre but stays inside, the total flux is still \(q/\varepsilon_0\), though the face fluxes become unequal; if the charge is moved outside the cube, the total flux through the cube is zero
C) If the charge is moved off-centre inside the cube, the total flux changes
D) If the charge is outside the cube, the total flux through the cube is \(q/\varepsilon_0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(q/6\varepsilon_0\) per face; total \(q/\varepsilon_0\) for any position inside; zero for a charge outside.
Given: \(\text{closed cubic surface; point charge q}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Gauss's law: }\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 1: \(\text{charge at the centre: by symmetry each of the 6 faces receives an equal share}\)
Step 2: \(\Phi_{\text{face}}=\dfrac{1}{6}\cdot\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{charge outside: }q_{\text{enc}}=0\Rightarrow\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=0\ (\text{field lines entering also leave})\]
Check: \[\text{charge inside but off-centre: }q_{\text{enc}}=q\Rightarrow\text{total}=q/\varepsilon_0\text{ still}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the total flux depends only on the enclosed charge, not on its position or the shape of the surface; the individual face fluxes depend on position}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(q/\varepsilon_0\text{ is the total, not the flux through each face}\); (C) \(\text{the total depends only on the enclosed charge}\); (D) \(\text{an outside charge encloses nothing}\).
Key point: \(\Phi_{\text{total}}=q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0;\ \text{symmetry shares it among faces}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Charge, voltage and stored energy for 2 µF and 3 µF capacitors connected in series and in parallel to 10 V
questions.question: Capacitors of 2.0 µF and 3.0 µF are connected (i) in series and (ii) in parallel across a 10 V battery. What are the equivalent capacitance, the charge on each capacitor and the total energy stored in each arrangement?
options: A) Series: 5.0 µF, 20 µC and 30 µC, 250 µJ; parallel: 1.2 µF, 12 µC each, 60 µJ
B) Series: 1.2 µF, 12 µC each, 120 µJ; parallel: 5.0 µF, 50 µC each, 500 µJ
C) Series: 1.2 µF, 12 µC on each (6.0 V and 4.0 V across them), 60 µJ; parallel: 5.0 µF, 20 µC and 30 µC, 250 µJ
D) Series: 1.2 µF, 6.0 µC on each, 30 µJ; parallel: 5.0 µF, 20 µC and 30 µC, 250 µJ
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Series: 1.2 µF, 12 µC each, 60 µJ; parallel: 5.0 µF, 20 and 30 µC, 250 µJ.
Given: \(C_1=2.0\ \mu\mathrm F,\ C_2=3.0\ \mu\mathrm F,\ V=10\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{series: }\dfrac1C=\dfrac1{C_1}+\dfrac1{C_2},\ \text{same Q};\ \text{parallel: }C=C_1+C_2,\ \text{same V};\ U=\tfrac12CV^2\)
Step 1: \(\text{series: }C=\dfrac{2\times3}{5}=1.2\ \mu\mathrm F;\ Q=12\ \mu\mathrm C;\ V_1=\dfrac{12}{2}=6.0\ \mathrm V,\ V_2=\dfrac{12}{3}=4.0\ \mathrm V\)
Step 2: \(U_s=\tfrac12\times1.2\times10^{-6}\times100=60\ \mu\mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{parallel: }C=5.0\ \mu\mathrm F;\ Q_1=20\ \mu\mathrm C,\ Q_2=30\ \mu\mathrm C;\ U_p=\tfrac12\times5.0\times10^{-6}\times100=250\ \mu\mathrm J\]
Check: \[\text{series: }6.0+4.0=10\ \mathrm V\ \checkmark;\ \text{parallel: }20+30=50\ \mu\mathrm C=5.0\times10\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in series the smaller capacitor takes the larger share of the voltage; in parallel each capacitor has the full voltage, so much more energy is stored}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{swaps the series and parallel rules}\); (B) \(\text{omits the factor }\tfrac12\text{ in the energy and puts equal charges in parallel}\); (D) \(\text{halves the series charge}\).
